units.title: How to read the Bible
units.eq: How does God speak in Scripture?

lessons.title: God’s word in human words
lessons.idea: God is the author of Scripture and the human writers are true authors who used their own gifts, style and world. We take both seriously: God’s word in human words. Because of this the Bible is without error in what God wanted to teach for our salvation.
lessons.question: If God is the author, why do the books differ in style?
lessons.activity: “Two accounts, one event” (30 min). Read the feeding of the five thousand in Matthew 14, Mark 6 and John 6 side by side. Students list shared details and differences. Ask what each author emphasizes and why. Conclude: the differences show human authors, the agreement shows one story God wants told.
teach: God is the author of Scripture; inspired human authors wrote “all and only” what he wanted (CCC 105–107; Dei Verbum 11). 2 Timothy 3:16 says all Scripture is “God-breathed.”
The human authors are “true authors” using their faculties and context (CCC 106). To read well we must ask what they meant (CCC 109–110).
Because the Spirit is the author, Scripture teaches “firmly, faithfully and without error” the truth for our salvation (CCC 107). This does not make it a science textbook.
The Church warns against fundamentalism, which ignores literary forms, and against skepticism, which denies inspiration.
talk: If God is the author, why do the books sound different?
Which passage raises questions for you?
quiz: Who is the author of Scripture?|Only angels|God, through human authors|Only humans|The Church alone|1|CCC 105-106.
Inerrancy means Scripture teaches…|Without error what God wanted for our salvation|Everything about science|Only poetry|Nothing|0|CCC 107.
Biblical authors are…|Ghostwriters|Unknown|Secretaries only|True authors|3|Dei Verbum 11.
lessons.life: Read one chapter of a Gospel slowly this week and write one question.
lessons.saint: Jerome: the scholar who said that ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.
misc: “God dictated every word like a secretary.”
“The Bible is just human opinion about God.”
lessons.mem: “All Scripture is inspired by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness.” (2 Timothy 3:16)
lessons.hook: Show a letter from a parent written in a child’s own handwriting style. “Whose is it?” Both. The Bible is like that: God’s message through real authors.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain in a few sentences how God and human authors both wrote Scripture.

script.open: Hold up a Bible. Ask, “Who wrote this?” Take answers (Moses, Paul, God). Say, “All of those answers are partly right. Today we find out how.”
teach: Read 2 Timothy 3:16 and 2 Peter 1:21. Say: “‘All Scripture is inspired by God’ and ‘men moved by the Holy Spirit spoke from God.’ Inspiration means God is the principal author of the Bible. He used real human authors, who wrote in their own language, style and setting, and he guided them so that they wrote all that he wanted written and nothing more. Think of a musician and an instrument, except that the human authors were free and active, not instruments only.”

Say: “Because God is the author, Scripture teaches truth without error: the truth God wanted put in writing for our salvation. This is called inerrancy. Because people are the authors, we must pay attention to who was writing, to whom, in what time and in what form. The Bible is both fully divine and fully human, a little like Jesus, who is both God and man. This is why Dei Verbum, the Second Vatican Council’s document on Scripture, speaks of God’s word in human words.”

Say: “The Catholic Bible has 73 books: 46 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New. The Church recognized which books belong in the canon, the official list, by the Spirit’s guidance, at councils in the late fourth century. The Church did not invent the Bible, but she discerned which writings were inspired. Catholic Bibles include seven Old Testament books that many Protestant Bibles omit: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and 1 and 2 Maccabees. Jerome’s Latin translation is the Vulgate.”
ask: What does inspiration mean? (God is the principal author; he guided human authors.)
How many books are in the Catholic Bible? (73.)
Why do we have to read the Bible with attention to the human authors? (They wrote in a time, place and form.)
practice: Pairs read 2 Timothy 3:16 and 2 Peter 1:21 aloud.
On a sheet, draw two columns: “God’s part” and “The human author’s part.”
Fill each with what the verses and the lesson say.
Write one sentence explaining inspiration to a younger child.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, open our hearts to your word.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Find the table of contents in a Bible and count the books with someone.”

tryit: Read 2 Timothy 3:16 and 2 Peter 1:21.
Write who the authors are, and who the Author is.
Explain inspiration in your own words.
lessons.saintStory:
Jerome was born around 347 in Dalmatia and studied in Rome. He was brilliant, and quick-tempered. After a dream in which he felt accused of loving classical writers more than Christ, he gave himself to Scripture. He spent years as a hermit in the Syrian desert, where he taught himself Hebrew.
In Rome, Pope Damasus asked him to produce a reliable Latin Bible. Jerome later settled in Bethlehem, near the cave of Jesus’ birth, and worked for over thirty years translating the Old Testament from Hebrew and revising the New. His translation, the Vulgate, was the Church’s standard Bible for more than a thousand years.
He wrote, “Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.” He died in 420 in Bethlehem.

lessons.title: Literary forms and the senses of Scripture
lessons.idea: To understand Scripture we must notice the literary form (history, poetry, law, prophecy, parable, letter, apocalypse) and read for the senses of Scripture: the literal sense, and the spiritual senses (allegorical, moral, anagogical).
lessons.question: What is the difference between literal and spiritual senses?
lessons.activity: “Form sort and the four senses” (30 min). Cards with Bible passages (Genesis 1, Leviticus 19, Psalm 23, Isaiah 53, Matthew 5, Romans 8, Revelation 21). Students sort by form. Then take Jonah’s three days: literal (what happens), allegorical (Christ’s tomb, Matthew 12:40), moral (obey God), anagogical (resurrection hope).
teach: Read with attention to literary genres and the author’s intention (CCC 109–110). Genesis 1 uses a literary structure to teach that God is the source and all is good.
The literal sense is what the words convey (CCC 116). The spiritual senses build on it: allegorical (how events point to Christ), moral (how to act) and anagogical (heavenly destiny) (CCC 115–117).
In Luke 24:25–27 Jesus explains how “all the Scriptures” point to him. The Old Testament is fulfilled in him (CCC 128–130).
Read all of Scripture in the light of Christ, the unity of the whole Bible and the Church’s living Tradition (CCC 112–114).
talk: How does knowing the genre change reading?
quiz: The literal sense is…|What the author intended to say|An allegory only|A scientific reading|A fantasy|0|CCC 116.
The senses of Scripture are literal and…|Scientific|Silly|Spiritual|Political|2|CCC 115.
Wisdom literature includes…|Genesis|Acts|Proverbs and Job|Exodus|2|CCC 120.
lessons.life: Identify the genre of tonight’s reading before you read it.
lessons.saint: Augustine: the teacher who learned to read Scripture in the light of Christ.
misc: “Reading a text figuratively means it is not true.”
lessons.mem: “Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.” (Luke 24:27)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Do you read a recipe the way you read a poem?” Read two lines of different kinds and ask how each should be taken.
lessons.assess: Give a passage and ask students to name its literary form and one spiritual sense.

script.open: Read three short pieces aloud with no labels: a line of a poem, a line from a news report, a line from a joke. Ask, “How did you know how to take each?” Say, “The Bible has the same variety.”
teach: Say: “The Bible is a library of many literary forms. There is history (1 and 2 Kings), law (Leviticus), poetry and song (Psalms), wisdom sayings (Proverbs), prophecy (Isaiah), Gospel (Mark), letters (Romans), and apocalyptic writing (Revelation). We read each according to its form. We would not read a poem as a newspaper report. Asking what the author intended, in that form, is the literal sense, the foundation of all interpretation.”

Say: “Parables are short stories with a point. Genesis 1 is a theological account of creation, using the language of a week and a pattern of days to teach that God made everything good and gave us the Sabbath. It is not a science textbook. History in the Bible is true history told for faith, and the authors sometimes arrange events to teach. The Church warns us not to pit Scripture against science, since truth cannot contradict truth.”

Say: “Beyond the literal sense, the Church speaks of three spiritual senses. The allegorical sense sees how events point to Christ: the crossing of the Red Sea points to Baptism. The moral sense shows how to act: Israel’s wandering teaches us to trust God. The anagogical sense points to our final destiny in heaven: Jerusalem as a sign of heaven. The literal sense comes first, and the spiritual senses are built upon it.”
ask: Name three literary forms in the Bible. (History, poetry, prophecy, Gospel, letter.)
What is the literal sense? (What the human author intended to say in that form.)
What are the three spiritual senses? (Allegorical, moral, anagogical.)
practice: Give small groups passages: Psalm 23, Luke 15:11-32, Proverbs 10:1-5, 1 Kings 3:16-28, 1 Corinthians 13, Genesis 1:1-5.
Each group names the form and says what to look for in that form.
Pick one passage and find its literal sense in one sentence, then one spiritual sense.
Share with the class.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, as we read your word, help us to understand it.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Before you read a Bible passage this week, ask what kind of writing it is.”

tryit: Sort passages by literary form.
Name the form.
Say how it changes what you look for.
lessons.saintStory:
Augustine was born in 354 in North Africa. As a young man he was clever, ambitious and restless. He found the Bible rough and unsophisticated compared to the writers he admired, and he turned away from it for years.
In Milan, he heard the bishop Ambrose preach, and was surprised to learn that texts that had seemed foolish to him had deeper meanings. Ambrose taught him that Old Testament stories could be read as pointing to Christ. Augustine began to read the Bible again, and in 386, in a garden, he heard a child’s voice saying, “Take and read.” He opened Romans 13 and was converted.
As bishop of Hippo he wrote a guide to interpreting Scripture. He said that the New Testament is hidden in the Old, and the Old is revealed in the New.

lessons.title: Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium
lessons.idea: Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium work together. Scripture and Tradition flow from the same divine source; the Magisterium (the Pope and bishops) authentically interprets them. None stands alone.
lessons.question: Why do Catholics rely on Tradition as well as the Bible?
lessons.activity: “Three witnesses” (25 min). Students use Acts 2:42, 2 Thessalonians 2:15 and the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15) to show how apostles taught by word and writing, and decided disputes with authority. Draw a diagram with arrows among Scripture, Tradition, Magisterium. Explain it to a partner.
teach: Sacred Tradition and Sacred Scripture “flow out of the same divine wellspring” (CCC 80–82). Tradition is the living transmission of the Gospel, not just customs.
The Church wrote the New Testament and determined the canon under the Spirit’s guidance (CCC 120). The Magisterium is “not above the Word of God, but serves it” (CCC 86).
Paul told the Thessalonians to “hold to the traditions you were taught, whether by word of mouth or by letter” (2 Thessalonians 2:15). Acts 15 shows a council deciding authoritatively.
Contrast gently with the Protestant principle sola scriptura, which the Church does not accept, but avoid caricature.
talk: Why does the Church read Scripture with Tradition?
quiz: The deposit of faith is…|Scripture and Tradition|Only Tradition|Opinions|Only Scripture|0|CCC 84.
The Magisterium is…|A council only|A hymn|A book|The teaching office of the Church|3|CCC 85.
Tradition is…|A story|A custom|The Gospel handed on|A rule|2|CCC 78.
lessons.life: Learn who the successor of Peter and your bishop are.
lessons.saint: Irenaeus: the bishop who pointed to the apostles’ teaching, handed down.
misc: “Tradition means old customs that can change anytime.”
“The Church put the Bible above itself.”
lessons.mem: “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” (Acts 2:42)
lessons.hook: Show a three-legged stool, then remove a leg. “What happens?” Use it as a way to picture how the three support each other (while noting the analogy is limited).
lessons.assess: Ask students to define each of the three and explain how they fit together.

script.open: Play a game of whispers: pass a short sentence down a line of six students. Compare the first and last. Ask, “How could the Church be sure that Jesus’ teaching was handed down without being changed?”
teach: Say: “Jesus did not write a book. He taught, healed, and formed the apostles, and he sent them: ‘Go therefore and make disciples… teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you.’ (Matthew 28:19-20) The apostles passed on his teaching by preaching, by example and by writing. Some of that was written down by inspired authors and became the New Testament. The rest continued as living practice and teaching.”

Say: “Sacred Tradition is the living handing-on of the Gospel from the apostles, through the Church, by the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition flow from the same source, God’s revelation, and the Church accepts both with equal reverence. Paul wrote, ‘Stand firm and hold to the traditions which you were taught by us, either by word of mouth or by letter.’ (2 Thessalonians 2:15) Tradition is not a set of old customs. It is the Gospel, living in the Church.”

Say: “The Magisterium is the Church’s teaching office: the Pope and the bishops in union with him. Jesus gave Peter and the apostles the task of teaching with authority, and promised, ‘He who hears you hears me.’ (Luke 10:16) The Magisterium is not above God’s word, but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on. Together the three work like a three-legged stool: Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium. Take one away and the stool falls.”
ask: What is Sacred Tradition? (The living handing-on of the Gospel from the apostles.)
What is the Magisterium? (The Church’s teaching office: the Pope and bishops.)
How do Scripture, Tradition and Magisterium fit? (They work together, and the Magisterium serves the word.)
practice: Draw a three-legged stool. Label each leg.
Under each, write what it gives and a verse: Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16), Tradition (2 Thessalonians 2:15), Magisterium (Luke 10:16).
On the seat, write “the Gospel, whole and unchanged.”
Explain to a partner what would happen if one leg were missing.
script.close: Pray the Creed together slowly. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask someone where they learned the faith, and who taught them.”

tryit: Draw the three-legged stool.
Write on each leg what it adds.
Explain why one leg alone would fall.
lessons.saintStory:
Irenaeus was born around 130 in Asia Minor. As a boy, he heard Polycarp of Smyrna, who had known the apostle John. Irenaeus later moved to Lyon, in Gaul, where he became bishop after the previous bishop was martyred.
Teachers were spreading false ideas called Gnosticism, claiming secret knowledge that was hidden from ordinary Christians. Irenaeus wrote a long work, Against Heresies, to answer them. He said the truth is not secret. It was given to the apostles, and handed on openly in the Church through the bishops, who could trace their succession back to them. He pointed to the Church in Rome as an example.
He died around 202. Irenaeus is a witness that the teaching we have is the teaching the apostles gave.

lessons.title: Creation: a gift
lessons.idea: Genesis 1–2 teach that God created everything freely and that all is good. Humans, made in his image, are the summit of creation and are called to care for the world. The Sabbath is the crown of creation.
lessons.question: What does Genesis 1 teach?
lessons.activity: “Genesis 1 theology chart” (30 min). Students read Genesis 1:1–2:4 and list the claims: one God, creation by word, order, goodness, humanity in God’s image, Sabbath. Compare with Babylonian creation myths (the gods fight and humans are slaves). What is different?
teach: Creation is a gift out of nothing, ordered and good (CCC 279–301). God needs nothing; creation is the first act of love.
Humans are created male and female in God’s image (Genesis 1:27; CCC 355–357). That gives every person equal dignity and the vocation to know and love God.
The Sabbath is the goal of creation; worship is built into the world (CCC 345–349). The second account (Genesis 2) shows the intimacy of God with Adam and Eve.
Caring for creation (stewardship) is a duty (CCC 2415–2418). Pope Francis’ Laudato Si’ develops this.
talk: What does Genesis 1 teach about God?
What does it teach about humans?
quiz: Creation ex nihilo means…|From a rock|Out of nothing|From a god|From chaos|1|CCC 296.
Humans are made…|Without a soul|In God’s image|From angels|By chance|1|CCC 355.
On the seventh day God…|Rested|Left|Destroyed|Created more|0|Genesis 2:2.
lessons.life: Keep a Sabbath rest from screens for a few hours.
lessons.saint: Kateri Tekakwitha: a young woman who saw God in the forest and the river.
misc: “Genesis 1 and 2 contradict each other, so the Bible is unreliable.”
“Humans may use creation however they want.”
lessons.mem: “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.” (Genesis 1:27)
lessons.hook: Play two clips: a news story about a storm and a video of a beautiful sunrise. “Both are in the same world. How can the world be good and still have trouble?” The next lessons answer.
lessons.assess: Ask students to list three truths taught by Genesis 1.

script.open: Take the class outside, or to a window. Ask them to be silent for one minute and notice five things made by God. Come back and share.
teach: Read Genesis 1:1-5, 26-31. Say: “‘In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.’ The Bible opens with God making everything out of nothing, simply by his word. The Church calls this creation ex nihilo, from nothing. God did not need anything to work with, and he did not make the world because he was lonely or needed it. He made it freely, out of love.”

Say: “Seven times Genesis says ‘God saw that it was good.’ After humans were made, ‘it was very good.’ Creation is good, because God made it. Matter is good. The body is good. Human beings are made in the image of God, which means we can think, choose and love, and we are made for relationship. God gave us dominion, which means care, not abuse. Genesis 2:15 says the man was placed in the garden ‘to till it and keep it.’ We are stewards of creation.”

Say: “The Genesis account is not a scientific account of how the world developed. It is a theological teaching about who made it, why, and what it means. The Church teaches that faith and science cannot truly contradict, since God is the author of both truth in nature and truth in Scripture. The Sabbath day, the seventh, is when God rested, and sets a pattern for us: work and then worship. Psalm 19:1: ‘The heavens declare the glory of God.’”
ask: What does creation from nothing mean? (God made everything by his word without any pre-existing material.)
What does ‘made in the image of God’ mean? (We can think, choose and love.)
What does being a steward mean? (Taking care of creation as God’s gift.)
practice: Pairs look out the window or go outside for five minutes.
On a sheet, list ten things God made that you saw or can think of.
Beside each, write one thing it shows about God (for example, “mountain: God is strong”).
Write a thank-you psalm line, for example, “Thank you, God, for ___.”
script.close: Pray Psalm 8:3-5 or the verse of Psalm 19:1. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do one thing this week to care for creation.”

tryit: Go outside or look at a window.
Write what you see that God made.
Write a thank-you line for each.
lessons.saintStory:
Kateri Tekakwitha was born in 1656 in a Mohawk village in what is now New York State. Her mother was an Algonquin Christian, and her father a Mohawk chief. When Kateri was four, smallpox killed her parents and little brother, and left her face scarred and her eyesight weak.
She lived with her uncle. When Jesuit missionaries visited, she listened to them, and she was baptized at twenty, on Easter Sunday, 1676. Some in her village disliked her faith, and she was threatened. She walked about two hundred miles to a Christian native village near Montreal.
There she prayed in the woods, where she set up crosses on trees, and she helped the sick and old. She died at twenty-four, in 1680. Kateri is the patron of ecology. She praised God in what God had made.

lessons.title: The fall
lessons.idea: Genesis 3 is the story of the fall: Adam and Eve, tempted by the serpent, chose their own way over God’s. The result was broken trust, shame, suffering and death. The Church calls the root of this original sin.
lessons.question: How does sin spread?
lessons.activity: “What, how, why” (25 min). In small groups, answer three questions from Genesis 3: What did they do? (disobeyed God’s command) How did it happen? (doubt: “Did God really say?”, pride) Why does it matter? (broken relationships with God, each other, creation). Then read Genesis 3:15 and Romans 5:18–19.
teach: Original sin is the first sin, a loss of original holiness, and its inheritance is a human nature wounded (CCC 396–405). It is transmitted by propagation, not imitation (CCC 404).
The temptation begins with doubt about God’s goodness (CCC 397). The result: shame, blame, pain, death and alienation (CCC 399–400).
Jesus is the new Adam who undoes the disobedience by his obedience (Romans 5:18–19; CCC 411). Baptism removes original sin (CCC 405).
The story is a true account in figurative language of a primeval event (CCC 390). Avoid fixating on the apple.
quiz: Original sin is…|A recent sin|A story|A state of fallen nature|A rule|2|CCC 404.
Concupiscence is…|Joy|Habit of prayer|Courage|Inclination to sin|3|CCC 405.
The first promise of a Redeemer is in…|Exodus 3|Psalm 23|Isaiah 7|Genesis 3:15|3|CCC 410.
lessons.life: Make an act of trust each time you notice temptation.
lessons.saint: Mary: the woman who said yes where Eve had said no.
misc: “Original sin means babies are guilty of a personal sin.”
lessons.mem: “As by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by one man’s obedience many will be made righteous.” (Romans 5:19)
lessons.hook: Show a broken mirror. “What breaks when we disobey?” Take answers and note that trust is the first thing to go.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what happened in the fall and what remedy God gave.

script.open: Ask, “Think of a time when you broke a rule that you knew was good. What was the reason? What happened next?” Take one or two answers. “Today we look at the first time this happened.”
teach: Read Genesis 2:15-17 and 3:1-13 in sections. Say: “God put Adam and Eve in the garden, gave them everything, and set one limit: not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The serpent, who stands for Satan, questioned God’s word. ‘Did God say…?’ He suggested that God was holding back, and told them they would be like God. Eve took the fruit, and Adam ate. Their eyes were opened, but only to see that they were naked and ashamed. They hid. When God asked, Adam blamed Eve, and Eve blamed the serpent.”

Say: “This is the story of the fall, and the Church calls the result original sin. The first humans, by their free choice, turned away from trusting God. Because of it, human nature was wounded, and we all inherit it: we are weakened in our will, drawn to evil, subject to suffering and death. Original sin is not a personal fault we commit, but a condition we are born into. Baptism removes it, but its effects remain. But God did not abandon them. In Genesis 3:15, he promises that the offspring of the woman will crush the serpent’s head. The Church calls this the first Gospel.”

Say: “Mary’s story answers Eve’s. Eve listened to the serpent and disobeyed; Mary listened to the angel and said yes. Through a woman came the fall; through a woman, the Savior. That is why the Church calls Mary the new Eve. And Jesus is the new Adam: Paul writes, ‘As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.’ (1 Corinthians 15:22) Where Adam failed in a garden, Jesus obeyed in another garden, Gethsemane.”
ask: What is original sin? (The wounded condition of human nature we inherit from the first sin.)
What did God promise in Genesis 3:15? (A Savior born of a woman who would defeat the serpent.)
Why is Mary called the new Eve? (She obeyed God where Eve disobeyed.)
practice: Draw a chart with two columns: Eve and Mary.
Fill in rows: Who spoke to her? What did he ask or say? What did she answer? What happened next?
At the bottom, add a row for Adam and Jesus.
Write one sentence that sums up what changed.
script.close: Pray the Hail Mary slowly. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Next time you hear the Hail Mary, think of Eve and Mary.”

tryit: Compare Eve’s story and Mary’s story.
Fill in the two columns.
Say what changed.
lessons.saintStory:
Mary was a young woman of Nazareth, engaged to Joseph, when the angel Gabriel appeared to her. He greeted her as “full of grace” and told her she would conceive and bear a son, Jesus, who would be great, and whose kingdom would have no end.
Mary asked, “How can this be, since I have no husband?” The angel said that the Holy Spirit would come upon her, and that nothing is impossible with God. Mary answered, “Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.”
The Fathers of the Church, such as Irenaeus, saw a parallel. Eve, in Eden, listened to the serpent and disobeyed. Mary, in Nazareth, listened to the angel and obeyed. Through Eve came the fall, and through Mary, the Savior. They call Mary the new Eve.

lessons.title: Cain and Abel; Noah; Babel
lessons.idea: In Genesis 4–11 sin spreads: Cain kills Abel, the world fills with violence and God sends the flood, and humans try to “make a name” at Babel. Yet God keeps saving: he protects Cain, rescues Noah’s family and makes a covenant, and finally calls Abram.
lessons.question: What do these stories show?
lessons.activity: “Timeline of Genesis 1–11” (25 min). Students draw a timeline with events and for each add: the sin, God’s response and the promise. Highlight the covenant sign: the rainbow (Genesis 9:12–17). End by asking, “Why does God choose Abram next?”
teach: Cain’s murder shows sin turning into hatred of a brother (CCC 2259). God asks, “Where is your brother?” God is a protector of life even for the guilty.
The flood story shows God’s judgment and mercy: Noah’s ark prefigures the Church and Baptism (CCC 56–58, 845, 1219; 1 Peter 3:20–21). The covenant with Noah includes all creation.
Babel shows human pride dividing nations; Pentecost reverses it (CCC 56, 674). God’s response is to start a new work with Abram.
The “remnant” theme runs through the Bible: God preserves a faithful few to renew the many.
quiz: God’s covenant with Noah included…|Only kings|Only Israel|All creation|Only priests|2|Genesis 9:9-10.
Babel shows…|Joy|Peace|Pride|Obedience|2|Genesis 11.
The flood story points to…|Passover|Pentecost|Baptism|Christmas|2|1 Peter 3:20-21.
lessons.life: Examine pride in your own heart.
lessons.saint: Noah: a righteous man who trusted God when no one else did.
lessons.mem: “I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood.” (Genesis 9:11)
lessons.hook: Draw a staircase going down with the labels Eden, Cain, Flood, Babel. Ask what pattern appears. Then add a second staircase going up with God’s mercy each time.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how each story shows both sin and God’s mercy.

script.open: Show a picture of a rainbow. Ask, “What do you think when you see one? Do you know where it comes from in the Bible?”
teach: Read Genesis 4:1-16 in summary. Say: “Cain and Abel each brought an offering. God accepted Abel’s but not Cain’s. Cain was angry, and God said, ‘If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door; its desire is for you, but you must master it.’ Cain did not listen. Sin was growing: from disobedience to murder in one generation. Yet even then God protected Cain with a mark. God’s mercy meets sin.”

Read Genesis 6:5-9:17 in summary. Say: “Violence filled the earth. God was grieved. But Noah found favor. He built the ark as God said. Eight people were saved through water. The Church sees this as a sign of Baptism (1 Peter 3:20-21). After the flood, God made a covenant: never again would a flood destroy all flesh. The rainbow is the sign. A covenant is a sacred bond between God and people. This one was with all creation.”

Read Genesis 11:1-9 in summary. Say: “At Babel, people said, ‘Let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves.’ They wanted to reach heaven by themselves. God confused their language and scattered them. The story shows that pride divides people. At Pentecost this is reversed: the Spirit comes, and each person hears the apostles in their own language. What pride scatters, the Spirit gathers.”
ask: What did God say to Cain about sin? (It is crouching at the door; master it.)
What is the sign of the covenant with Noah? (The rainbow.)
How does Pentecost answer Babel? (The Spirit gathers people of every language.)
practice: Fold a sheet into six boxes.
Draw the flood story in five pictures: the warning, building the ark, the flood, the dove, the rainbow.
In the sixth, draw Babel.
Under each, write one line on what it shows about sin or God’s mercy.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, you keep your promises. Thank you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look for a rainbow and remember God’s covenant.”

tryit: Tell the story of the flood in five pictures.
Add the sign of the rainbow.
Say what each story shows about sin and mercy.
lessons.saintStory:
After Adam and Eve, human wickedness spread. Cain, their son, was jealous of his brother Abel, because God accepted Abel’s offering. God warned Cain that sin was crouching at the door, but Cain killed Abel. When God asked where Abel was, Cain said, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” God said the blood cried out from the ground.
Generations later, the earth was full of violence. But Noah was a righteous man who walked with God. God told him to build an ark. It took years, and he was surely mocked. When the flood came, Noah, his family and the animals were saved. After the waters went down, God made a covenant with Noah and set his bow in the clouds as a sign that he would never again destroy the earth by flood.
Later at Babel, people built a tower to make a name for themselves, and God scattered them. Pride divides; trust in God saves.

units.title: The patriarchs
units.eq: How does God choose a people?

lessons.title: Abraham: father of faith
lessons.idea: God called Abram to leave home and promised him descendants, land and a blessing for all nations. Abraham believed, and it was counted to him as righteousness. He is the father of all who believe.
lessons.question: Why is Abraham our father in faith?
lessons.activity: “Abraham’s journey map” (30 min). Trace the route from Ur to Haran to Canaan to Egypt and back, marking altars, the covenant of Genesis 15 (stars, fire pot) and 17 (circumcision, name change). Write one sentence at each stop on what Abraham trusted.
teach: Abraham is “our father in faith” (CCC 59, 145–147; Romans 4). God’s call began a new people through whom the world would be blessed (Genesis 12:3).
In Genesis 15 God swears a covenant with fire passing between the animals: God takes the risk. Abraham “believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3).
Genesis 17 changes his name to Abraham, “father of a multitude.” Circumcision is the sign.
Abraham is honored by Jews, Christians and Muslims. Vatican II notes the Church’s special bond with Jews (CCC 839–840).
quiz: Abraham was told to…|Wait|Build a ship|Leave his country|Fight|2|Genesis 12:1.
God promised him…|Descendants and blessing|A throne|Gold|A tower|0|Genesis 12:2.
Abraham is called…|King of Egypt|Judge|Prophet of fire|Father of faith|3|Romans 4:11.
lessons.life: Take a faith step that scares you.
lessons.saint: Abraham: our father in faith, who left his home without knowing where he was going.
misc: “Abraham earned God’s favor by being good.”
“The promise to Abraham ended with the Old Testament.”
lessons.mem: “Abram believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness.” (Genesis 15:6)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Would you move to a place you’ve never seen because someone you trust asked you to?” Read Genesis 12:1–4.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name three parts of God’s promise to Abraham and how Abraham responded.

script.open: Say, “I’m going to ask you to pack and leave tomorrow for a place I won’t tell you. Would you go? What would you need to believe about me?” Let several answer. “Abraham did exactly this.”
teach: Read Genesis 12:1-4. Say: “God called Abram: ‘Go from your country… to the land that I will show you.’ The call came with three promises. Land: a home for his descendants. Descendants: a great nation. Blessing: ‘In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.’ And Abram went. The letter to the Hebrews says, ‘By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place which he was to receive as an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was to go.’ (Hebrews 11:8)”

Say: “Years went by and no child came. Abraham was ninety-nine and Sarah ninety when God promised again, and Sarah laughed. But the child came. God made a covenant with Abraham, sealed with circumcision, a sign in the flesh. A covenant is more than a contract: it makes the people family. Later, in Genesis 22, God asked Abraham to offer Isaac. This was a terrible test. Abraham trusted that God would keep his promise, even if he had to raise Isaac from the dead. God provided a ram. The Church sees here a sign of the Father offering his own Son.”

Say: “Abraham is a model of faith. Faith is not just believing facts. It is trusting God and acting on it, even when we can’t see the way. Paul writes, ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.’ (Romans 4:3) We pray in the Eucharistic Prayer: ‘our father Abraham.’ The promise to Abraham is fulfilled in Jesus. Through Christ, all nations are blessed.”
ask: What three promises did God make to Abraham? (Land, descendants, blessing for all nations.)
Why is Abraham a model of faith? (He trusted God and acted without seeing the way.)
What does Genesis 22 foreshadow? (The Father offering his Son.)
practice: Give each pair a blank map of the Middle East.
Mark the route: Ur to Haran to Canaan (Shechem, Bethel, Hebron) and Egypt.
Label the three promises.
On the back, write: “What did trust cost Abraham? What does it cost me?”
script.close: Pray: “Lord, give us faith like Abraham’s.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do one thing this week that takes trust.”

tryit: Mark Abraham’s journey on a map.
Label the three promises.
Write what trust cost him.
lessons.saintStory:
Abraham, first named Abram, lived in Ur, a city in Mesopotamia, with his wife Sarai. They were old and had no children. God said to him, “Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house to the land that I will show you. I will make of you a great nation.” Abram went, at seventy-five, not knowing where.
He traveled to Canaan, and God promised the land to his descendants. Later God took him outside at night and said, “Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able. So shall your descendants be.” Abram believed the Lord. God changed their names to Abraham and Sarah, and when Abraham was a hundred, Isaac was born.
When Isaac was a boy, God tested Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac. Abraham obeyed, trusting God, and at the last moment an angel stopped him. Paul calls Abraham the father of all who believe.

lessons.title: Isaac and Jacob
lessons.idea: God’s promise passes from Abraham to Isaac and to Jacob. Isaac’s near sacrifice shows Abraham’s faith and foreshadows Christ. Jacob wrestles with God and receives the name Israel.
lessons.question: What does Jacob’s new name mean?
lessons.activity: “Patriarchs compared” (30 min). Make a chart for Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: calling, test, mistake, promise, name. Include Genesis 22 (Isaac), 28 (Jacob’s ladder) and 32 (wrestling). Add where Jesus echoes them: John 1:51 (ladder).
teach: Isaac is the child of promise, born when Abraham and Sarah were old. In Genesis 22 God tests Abraham, then provides a ram; the church fathers saw Isaac carrying wood as a type of Christ carrying the cross (CCC 2572).
God does not desire human sacrifice; the story ends by showing that God provides the offering. Abraham’s faith that “God will provide” is fulfilled in Jesus.
Jacob’s ladder (Genesis 28) and wrestling at the Jabbok (Genesis 32) show a persistent seeker; he is renamed Israel, “one who strives with God” (CCC 2573).
God works with flawed people. Jacob was a deceiver, yet God kept his promise.
talk: What do we learn from Genesis 22?
How does God use flawed people?
quiz: God provided…|A goat|A ram|A bull|A lamb of silver|1|Genesis 22:13.
Jacob’s new name is…|Joseph|Isaac|Judah|Israel|3|Genesis 32:28.
Isaac foreshadows…|Elijah|Christ|Moses|David|1|CCC 2572.
lessons.life: Offer one thing to God this week.
lessons.saint: Jacob: the man who wrestled with God and received a new name.
lessons.mem: “God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” (Genesis 22:8)
lessons.hook: Read Genesis 22:1–2 and stop. Ask students to describe how Abraham felt. Then read the rest quickly and ask: “What did God show?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how Genesis 22 points to Christ.

script.open: Ask, “Have you ever had to say sorry to someone you wronged and were afraid of how they’d respond? Jacob did.”
teach: Say: “Isaac was Abraham’s promised son. His son Jacob had a complicated life. He cheated his brother Esau out of the birthright and the blessing. God did not choose Jacob because he was perfect. God’s promise continued through flawed people. It is grace, not merit. Jacob fled and slept at Bethel, where he had the dream of the ladder. God was with him, though he’d done wrong. The Church sees the ladder as a sign of Christ, who joins heaven and earth. (John 1:51)”

Say: “Years later, Jacob was heading home and feared Esau. Genesis 32 says he wrestled with a man all night. At dawn, he said, ‘I will not let you go, unless you bless me.’ The man gave him a new name: Israel, which means ‘he who strives with God.’ He limped afterward. It was a night of struggle and prayer, and he was changed. The next day, Esau ran to meet him and embraced him. They were reconciled.”

Say: “Jacob had twelve sons, who became the twelve tribes of Israel. One of them, Judah, is the ancestor of David and of Jesus. Jacob’s story teaches that God keeps his promises despite human weakness, that we can wrestle with God in prayer, and that God can change a person. Notice: Jesus chose twelve apostles, a sign of the new Israel.”
ask: Why did God’s promise continue through Jacob? (It depends on God’s grace, not Jacob’s goodness.)
What new name did Jacob receive? (Israel.)
What did the twelve sons become? (The twelve tribes of Israel.)
practice: Draw a timeline of Jacob’s life on a long sheet: birthright, blessing, Bethel, Laban, marriage, return, wrestling, reconciliation.
Mark with a star each place where God meets Jacob.
Circle the turning point.
Write two sentences: What changed Jacob? What helps change me?
script.close: Pray: “Lord, I will not let you go until you bless me.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray about one hard thing tonight.”

tryit: Make a timeline of Jacob’s life.
Mark where God meets him.
Explain what changed him.
lessons.saintStory:
Jacob was the younger twin son of Isaac and Rebekah. He was clever and ambitious. When his older brother Esau came in hungry, Jacob persuaded him to trade his birthright for a bowl of stew. Later, with his mother’s help, he tricked his blind father Isaac into giving him the blessing meant for Esau. Furious, Esau planned to kill him, so Jacob fled.
On the way, he slept with a stone for a pillow, and dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven, with angels going up and down. God promised him the land and descendants. Jacob woke and said, “Surely the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.” He went to work for his uncle Laban, was himself tricked, and married Leah and Rachel. After twenty years, he returned.
The night before he met Esau, he wrestled with a man until dawn. The man touched his hip, and said, “Your name shall no more be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God.” Jacob walked away limping, blessed. His twelve sons became the twelve tribes of Israel.

lessons.title: Joseph: from slavery to rescue
lessons.idea: Joseph, sold by his brothers, rose from slavery to rule Egypt and saved his family from famine. He forgave them and said, “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” His story shows divine providence.
lessons.question: How does Joseph forgive?
lessons.activity: “Role-play Genesis 45” (30 min). Act the reunion scene: Joseph reveals himself, the brothers react, Joseph forgives. Discuss: How does forgiveness change the story? Compare with Jesus’ forgiveness from the Cross.
teach: Joseph’s story takes the family from Canaan to Egypt (Genesis 37–50). It sets the stage for the Exodus.

God’s providence: he guides all things to their end without removing human freedom (CCC 302–314). Evil is never willed by God but he can draw good from it (CCC 311–312). “You meant evil against me; but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20).
Joseph is a type of Christ: beloved son, betrayed by brothers, sold, raised from a pit to save the people (CCC 128–130).
Speak carefully on suffering: this verse does not justify abuse. God works through but does not cause the evil of others.
talk: Where do you see good from evil?
quiz: Joseph was sold by…|Potiphar|Moses|His brothers|Pharaoh|2|Genesis 37.
Joseph said God meant it for…|Loss|Good|Fame|Evil|1|Genesis 50:20.
Providence is…|God’s care for creation|Fate|Control|Luck|0|CCC 302.
lessons.life: Forgive someone who has hurt you.
lessons.saint: Joseph, son of Jacob: sold by his brothers, he forgave them and saved them.
lessons.mem: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” (Genesis 50:20)
lessons.hook: Show a brightly colored coat. Ask, “What happens when a family has favorites?” Read the story of the coat in Genesis 37.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain providence using Joseph and to name one way Joseph is like Jesus.

script.open: Ask, “Has anything bad ever happened to you that, later, turned out to lead to something good? Not everything can be explained that way, but let’s see what Joseph found.”
teach: Read Genesis 37 in summary. Say: “Joseph’s brothers hated him: he was their father’s favorite, with the special coat, and he told them his dreams. They plotted to kill him, but sold him instead. A young man was alone in a foreign land. The story shows jealousy at work, and how sin spreads: lying to their father, and living with the guilt for years.”

Read Genesis 39-41 in summary. Say: “In Egypt, Joseph was faithful. When Potiphar’s wife tried to seduce him, he refused, saying, ‘How can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?’ He was thrown in prison unjustly. But ‘the Lord was with Joseph.’ In time, he was brought before Pharaoh, interpreted his dreams, and was made governor. It took thirteen years. Joseph never gave up trusting God.”

Read Genesis 45:1-8 and 50:15-21 in summary. Say: “When his brothers came, Joseph could have taken revenge. Instead he wept, and said, ‘Do not be distressed… for God sent me before you to preserve life.’ After their father died, the brothers feared he would punish them. Joseph said, ‘Do not fear… you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good.’ Joseph is a type, or foreshadowing, of Jesus: loved by his father, betrayed by his brothers for silver, handed over to foreigners, raised to glory, and became the savior of those who wronged him.”
ask: Why did the brothers sell Joseph? (Jealousy.)
How did Joseph respond to his brothers? (He forgave them, and saw God’s plan.)
How is Joseph like Jesus? (Betrayed by his brothers, raised up, and saved them.)
practice: Draw a line with ups and downs.
Mark the stages: favorite son, pit, slavery, prison, governor, reunion.
Under each “down,” write how Joseph stayed faithful.
At the end, write what Joseph said to his brothers in your own words.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, help me to forgive as Joseph did.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Forgive one person who hurt you.”

tryit: Trace the stages of Joseph’s story.
Mark each fall and rise.
Write what he said to his brothers.
lessons.saintStory:
Joseph was Jacob’s favorite son, and his brothers resented him. He had dreams that he would rule over them. One day, when he was seventeen, they threw him into a pit, then sold him to merchants who took him to Egypt. They told their father that a wild animal had killed him.
In Egypt, Joseph served in Potiphar’s house, but he was falsely accused and thrown in prison. There he interpreted the dreams of two officials. Two years later, when Pharaoh had troubling dreams, Joseph was called. He explained that seven good years would be followed by seven years of famine, and advised storing grain. Pharaoh made him second in command of Egypt.
When the famine came, his brothers traveled to Egypt to buy grain, not knowing who he was. After testing them, Joseph revealed himself, weeping. He said, “You meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive.” The whole family moved to Egypt.

units.title: Exodus and the Law
units.eq: How does God save and teach?

lessons.title: The call of Moses
lessons.idea: God heard Israel’s cry in Egypt and called Moses at the burning bush. He revealed his name, “I AM WHO I AM” (YHWH), and promised to be with his people and set them free.
lessons.question: How does God reveal his name?
lessons.activity: “The name” study (25 min). Read Exodus 3:1–15. Students write what the bush, the sandals, the name and Moses’ excuses show. Note how the Jews revere the name (“Adonai”). Compare with Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John (e.g., 8:58; 6:35).
teach: God reveals his name YHWH, “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14; CCC 203–213). It expresses that God is, he is faithful and he is with us.
The Jews avoid pronouncing the name; the Church follows by reading “Lord” (CCC 209). Jesus’ “I am” echoes the divine name (John 8:58; CCC 211).
God calls Moses despite his reluctance. The call shows that God sends the weak (Exodus 3:11). The holy ground teaches reverence (CCC 2144).
Present God as both transcendent (fire) and near (he hears).
talk: What does God say about suffering?
quiz: God’s name is revealed as…|Lord of war|The Great One|King|I AM|3|Exodus 3:14.
Moses was called at…|Mt Zion|Babel|The burning bush|The Red Sea|2|Exodus 3.
God hears…|Kings|Priests|Nobody|The cry of his people|3|Exodus 3:7.
lessons.life: Use God’s name only in prayer and respect.
lessons.saint: Moses: a shy shepherd who spoke with God at a burning bush.
lessons.mem: “I am who I am… Say this to the people of Israel: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” (Exodus 3:14)
lessons.hook: Ask, “What do you do when you hear someone calling for help?” Read Exodus 3:7–8: “I have seen the affliction of my people.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what God’s name tells us about him.

script.open: Light a candle and set it in front of the class. Ask, “What would you do if you saw a bush on fire that did not burn up?” Then say, “Moses had been a shepherd for forty years, and was about to meet God.”
teach: Read Exodus 3:1-10. Say: “God said, ‘I have seen the affliction of my people… and I have heard their cry… I know their sufferings, and I have come down to deliver them.’ Notice the verbs: seen, heard, know, come down. God is not distant. He sees suffering and acts. But he chooses to act through a person: ‘Come, I will send you to Pharaoh.’ God often saves through people he calls.”

Say: “Moses had excuses. ‘Who am I?’ God said, ‘I will be with you.’ ‘What is your name?’ God said, ‘I AM WHO I AM.’ This is the sacred name, written YHWH, which Jews do not pronounce out of reverence. It means God is, and is always present, the source of all being. ‘Please send someone else.’ Even Moses’ reluctance did not stop God. He gave his brother Aaron to speak for him. Notice that God’s call is never only a command. It comes with a promise to help.”

Say: “The burning bush also teaches us about holiness. ‘Take off your shoes, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.’ God’s presence makes a place holy and calls for reverence. Moses hid his face. The Church sees in the bush that burned without being consumed a sign of Mary, who carried God without being harmed. For us, this teaches reverence in church, at Mass, and before the Blessed Sacrament.”
ask: What four verbs does God use of himself in Exodus 3:7-8? (Seen, heard, know, come down.)
What does God’s name ‘I AM’ mean? (God is, the source of all being, always present.)
What did God promise Moses? (I will be with you.)
practice: Read Exodus 3:1-15 aloud with parts: narrator, God, Moses.
On a sheet, list everything the passage says about who God is.
In a second list, write Moses’ excuses and God’s answers.
Write one thing God might be asking of you, and one excuse you might make.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, you are with us. Take away our fear.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Take off your shoes, in your heart, when you pray.”

tryit: Read Exodus 3:1-15 aloud in parts.
List what God says about himself.
Say what God asked Moses to do.
lessons.saintStory:
Moses was born in Egypt, when Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew baby boy to be thrown into the Nile. His mother hid him for three months, then placed him in a basket among the reeds. Pharaoh’s daughter found him and raised him as her son. Moses grew up in the palace, but he knew he was a Hebrew.
One day he killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew slave, and fled to Midian, where he became a shepherd and married Zipporah. For forty years he lived quietly. One day, he saw a bush burning but not consumed. A voice said, “Moses, Moses! Take off your shoes, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.”
God said, “I have seen the affliction of my people… I will send you to Pharaoh.” Moses said, “Who am I?” and “I am slow of speech.” God promised, “I will be with you.” And when Moses asked God’s name, God answered, “I AM WHO I AM.”

lessons.title: Passover and the Red Sea
lessons.idea: The Passover and the crossing of the Red Sea are Israel’s great salvation events. The lamb’s blood saved the firstborn, and God split the sea. Christians see the Passover fulfilled in Christ the Lamb and the Exodus in Baptism and the Eucharist.
lessons.question: How does Passover foreshadow Easter?
lessons.activity: “Passover to Eucharist” (30 min). Make a chart linking the elements: lamb → Lamb of God (John 1:29), blood on doorposts → blood of Christ, unleavened bread → Eucharistic bread, sea → Baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1–4). Then compare Exodus 12 to the Last Supper (Luke 22:7–20).
teach: Passover: the lamb, the blood, the unleavened bread, the haste (Exodus 12). It is celebrated each year as a memorial (CCC 1363). Israel remembers as if present.
The Red Sea is the climax: God saves by water and defeats Pharaoh (Exodus 14). The Fathers saw it as a type of Baptism (CCC 1221–1222).
Jesus is “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). He died at Passover; the Last Supper was a Passover meal and the Mass is its new fulfillment (CCC 1340, 1363–1364).
The Easter Vigil reads Exodus 14. Point out the link.
talk: How is the Last Supper a Passover?
quiz: The blood of the lamb…|Saved the firstborn|Cleaned the house|Was thrown away|Fed Israel|0|Exodus 12:13.
Christ is the…|Judge|Shepherd of sheep|Lamb of God|King of kings only|2|John 1:29.
Israel crossed the…|Jordan|Dead Sea|Nile|Red Sea|3|Exodus 14.
lessons.life: Read Exodus 12 and John 1 and compare.
lessons.saint: Miriam: the sister of Moses who led the women in song at the sea.
misc: “Passover is only a Jewish festival with nothing to do with Christians.”
“The Last Supper was a normal dinner.”
lessons.mem: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29)
lessons.hook: Set out a plate with lamb (or a picture), unleavened bread, bitter herbs. Ask what each tells about being rescued in haste.
lessons.assess: Ask students to match three Passover elements with their fulfillment in Christ.

script.open: Ask, “What would you eat on the night before the most important journey of your life? Why would you eat it in a hurry?”
teach: Read Exodus 11-12 in summary. Say: “God sent ten plagues on Egypt, but Pharaoh would not let the people go. The tenth was the death of the firstborn. God told Israel to take a lamb without blemish, kill it, and put its blood on the doorposts. ‘When I see the blood, I will pass over you.’ They were to eat the lamb roasted, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, dressed for travel. This was the first Passover. That night, Pharaoh let them go.”

Read Exodus 14. Say: “Then Pharaoh changed his mind and chased them. The people were trapped between the army and the sea, and were afraid. Moses said, ‘Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the Lord.’ The sea parted. Israel walked through on dry ground. The waters returned and drowned the Egyptians. Israel sang. God had saved them. They passed from slavery to freedom through water.”

Say: “The Passover is celebrated every year by the Jewish people. The Church sees in it a sign of what Jesus did. Jesus is the Lamb of God (John 1:29), whose blood saves us. His Last Supper was a Passover meal. On the cross, he was the sacrificial Lamb. At the Mass, we receive the Lamb. The Red Sea is a sign of Baptism: we pass through water from slavery to sin to freedom. The Easter Vigil reads this story every year.”
ask: What saved the Israelites in Egypt? (The blood of the lamb on the doorposts.)
What did God do at the sea? (He parted it, and Israel passed through on dry ground.)
What does the Red Sea foreshadow? (Baptism.)
practice: Set out cards with the events: plagues, lamb and blood, unleavened bread, midnight, Exodus, chased, Red Sea, song.
Put them in order.
In a second column, match each to what it points to: lamb (Jesus), blood (his sacrifice), bread (Eucharist), sea (Baptism).
Write a short song line like Miriam’s in thanksgiving for being saved.
script.close: Sing or recite “Behold the Lamb of God.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask your family what Easter means to you.”

tryit: Put the ten plagues and the Passover in order.
Match each Passover element to the Eucharist.
Write a song line for the Red Sea.
lessons.saintStory:
Miriam was the older sister of Moses and Aaron. As a girl, she watched from among the reeds when her baby brother’s basket was put in the Nile. When Pharaoh’s daughter found him, Miriam stepped forward and asked, “Shall I go and call you a nurse from the Hebrew women?” She brought her own mother, who nursed Moses.
Years later, after the Israelites crossed the Red Sea and Pharaoh’s army was swept away, Miriam, called a prophetess, took a tambourine, and all the women followed her with tambourines and dancing. She sang, “Sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.”
She traveled with the people through the wilderness, and died at Kadesh. Her song is the oldest in the Bible and is sung again at the Easter Vigil.

lessons.title: Sinai: the Law and covenant
lessons.idea: At Sinai, after saving Israel, God gave the Law as the way of covenant life. The Ten Commandments are a gift of freedom, summarizing love of God and love of neighbor.
lessons.question: How are the Ten Commandments a gift?
lessons.activity: “Commandments by theme” (25 min). Cards with the ten commandments; students sort into “love of God” (1–3) and “love of neighbor” (4–10) and rewrite each in one positive sentence. Then read Exodus 19:3–6 and 20:1–2 and note that God first rescues, then gives the law.
teach: God gave the Law after saving Israel (Exodus 20:2; CCC 2056–2063). It is a gift of freedom, not a price for salvation.
The Decalogue is divided in two tablets: love of God and love of neighbor (CCC 2067–2068). All people are bound by it because it expresses natural law (CCC 2070–2072).
Israel became “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6). The covenant is a relationship.
Our numbering follows Augustine; Jews and Protestants number differently. Mention it for curious students.
talk: Why did God give the Law?
quiz: The Ten Commandments were given at…|Jericho|Mount Carmel|Jordan|Mount Sinai|3|Exodus 19-20.
They begin with…|Love of self|Wealth|Love of God|Rules for kings|2|CCC 2083.
The Law is…|Obsolete|A trap|A gift|A burden only|2|CCC 2059.
lessons.life: Say the Ten Commandments aloud.
lessons.saint: Bezalel: the craftsman God filled with his Spirit to build the meeting tent.
misc: “We keep the commandments to earn God’s love.”
lessons.mem: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” (Exodus 20:2)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Do rules make us free or boxed in? What about traffic rules?” Reflect that rules make life together possible and free.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain why God gave the commandments after the Exodus, not before.

script.open: Ask, “When someone gives you rules, do you ever feel like they are against you? Think about a game: do rules make it worse or make it possible?”
teach: Read Exodus 19-20 in summary. Say: “Three months after leaving Egypt, Israel came to Mount Sinai. God spoke from fire and cloud. He offered a covenant: ‘If you will obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my own possession among all peoples.’ The people answered, ‘All that the Lord has spoken we will do.’ Notice the order. God first saved them, and then gave the Law. The Ten Commandments begin, ‘I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.’ The Law is the response of a free people, not the price of freedom.”

Say: “The Ten Commandments, or Decalogue, are written on two tablets. The first three are about love of God: no other gods, do not take his name in vain, keep the Sabbath holy. The other seven are about love of neighbor: honor your father and mother, do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, do not covet your neighbor’s wife, do not covet your neighbor’s goods. Jesus summarized them: love God and love your neighbor.”

Say: “Soon after, while Moses was on the mountain, the people made a golden calf and worshiped it. This was a breaking of the covenant. Moses interceded for them, and God forgave. God then renewed the covenant. The tabernacle, with its beautiful furnishings made by Bezalel, was the sign that God would dwell with them. The Law is a gift: it shows the path of life, and it protects freedom and love. Jesus said, ‘If you love me, you will keep my commandments.’ (John 14:15)”
ask: Why did God give the Law after the Exodus? (It was the response of a free people to God who saved them.)
How are the two tablets divided? (Love of God and love of neighbor.)
What happened at the golden calf? (Israel broke the covenant; God forgave.)
practice: Draw two tablets on a sheet.
On the first, write the first three commandments; on the second, the other seven.
Beside each, write one way to keep it today.
At the bottom, write what Jesus says is the summary.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, your law is a lamp for my feet.” (Psalm 119:105.) Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Learn the Ten Commandments in order.”

tryit: Sort the Ten Commandments into two tablets.
Write the matching Beatitude or New Law teaching.
Say why God gave the Law after freeing Israel.
lessons.saintStory:
After the Israelites left Egypt, they camped at the foot of Mount Sinai. God called Moses up the mountain and gave him the Ten Commandments, written on two stone tablets. He also gave instructions for a tent of meeting, the tabernacle, where God would dwell among his people, and for the ark of the covenant to hold the tablets.
God said to Moses, “I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri… and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship.” Bezalel worked in gold, silver, bronze, wood and stone. With another craftsman, Oholiab, he made the ark, the lampstand, the altar and the priestly garments.
He is the first person in the Bible said to be filled with the Spirit. His story shows that God gives gifts for worship, and that beauty serves holiness.

units.title: Kings and prophets
units.eq: How does God lead his people?

lessons.title: Samuel, Saul and David
lessons.idea: Israel asked for a king. After Saul failed, God chose David, a shepherd, “a man after his own heart.” God promised David an everlasting throne, a promise fulfilled in Jesus, Son of David.
lessons.question: What did God promise David?
lessons.activity: “David to Jesus family tree” (25 min). Draw a simple tree from David (1 Samuel 16) through Solomon to Joseph and Jesus (Matthew 1). Mark God’s promise in 2 Samuel 7:12–16 and the title “Son of David” (Matthew 1:1; Luke 1:32–33).
teach: Samuel anoints Saul and then David (1 Samuel 9–16). David is shepherd, warrior, king and psalmist (CCC 2579).
God’s covenant with David (2 Samuel 7) promises an eternal dynasty (CCC 709). The angel tells Mary her son will receive “the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32).
David is a sinner too: Bathsheba and Uriah (2 Samuel 11–12). His repentance in Psalm 51 shows God’s mercy.
The Messiah (“anointed”) is the king from David’s line (CCC 436).
talk: How is Jesus the son of David?
quiz: David was anointed by…|Samuel|Elijah|Moses|Nathan|0|1 Samuel 16.
God promised David…|A city|A temple of gold|Peace only|An eternal throne|3|2 Samuel 7:16.
Messiah means…|Lord|King|Teacher|Anointed|3|CCC 436.
lessons.life: Pray a psalm of David.
lessons.saint: David: a shepherd boy who became king, sinned deeply, and repented.
misc: “Kings in the Bible ruled by their own right.”
lessons.mem: “The Lord looks on the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)
lessons.hook: Show a shepherd’s staff and a crown. Ask, “Who would you choose to be king?” Read 1 Samuel 16:7: “The Lord looks on the heart.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how the promise to David points to Jesus.

script.open: Ask, “Who is the smallest, youngest person in your family? Would you choose them to lead? God chose David that way.”
teach: Read 1 Samuel 16:1-13 in summary. Say: “Samuel was sent to anoint a new king from Jesse’s sons. Samuel looked at the tallest and said, ‘Surely the Lord’s anointed is before him.’ But God said, ‘Do not look on his appearance… for the Lord sees not as man sees; man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart.’ The youngest, David, was brought in from the fields. ‘Arise, anoint him; for this is he.’ And the Spirit of the Lord came mightily upon David from that day.”

Read 1 Samuel 17 in summary. Say: “Goliath was a champion of the Philistines, over nine feet tall. For forty days he mocked Israel’s army, and nobody dared fight him. David, sent by his father with food for his brothers, heard him and said, ‘Who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?’ Saul tried to give him armor, but it was too heavy. David took his staff, five smooth stones and his sling. ‘The Lord who delivered me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will deliver me.’ One stone brought down the giant.”

Read 2 Samuel 11-12 in summary. Say: “David became king and was successful. But one night he saw Bathsheba and took her, and then arranged for her husband to be killed in battle. Nathan the prophet confronted him with a story of a rich man who stole a poor man’s lamb. David was furious. Nathan said, ‘You are the man.’ David said, ‘I have sinned against the Lord.’ He was forgiven, but there were consequences. Psalm 51 is his prayer of repentance: ‘Create in me a clean heart, O God.’ David is great not because he never sinned, but because he repented. And God’s promise to David is fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David.”
ask: How does God choose? (He looks at the heart.)
What gave David strength against Goliath? (Trust in the Lord.)
What did David do when Nathan confronted him? (He admitted his sin and repented.)
practice: Fold a sheet in four.
Draw four scenes: anointing, Goliath, king, Nathan.
Mark with a heart where David trusted God, and a cross where he fell.
Read Psalm 51:1-4 aloud and underline a line you could pray.
script.close: Pray Psalm 51:10: “Create in me a clean heart, O God.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray Psalm 51 before Confession.”

tryit: Tell David’s story in four scenes.
Mark where he trusted God and where he fell.
Read Psalm 51:1-4.
lessons.saintStory:
After the time of the judges, the people asked Samuel for a king like other nations. God chose Saul, but Saul disobeyed, and God sent Samuel to anoint another. Samuel went to Jesse in Bethlehem. Jesse’s seven older sons passed before him, but the Lord said, “Man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart.” The youngest, David, was out with the sheep. Samuel anointed him.
David later faced the giant Goliath, armed only with a sling and trust in God. “You come to me with a sword and spear, but I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts.” He became king, united the tribes and made Jerusalem the capital. God promised that his house and throne would last forever.
But David also sinned gravely. He took Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and had Uriah killed. The prophet Nathan told him a parable, and said, “You are the man.” David said, “I have sinned against the Lord.” He repented, and wrote Psalm 51.

lessons.title: Solomon and the Temple
lessons.idea: Solomon built the Temple in Jerusalem as God’s house, where sacrifices were offered and the people met God. It prefigures Christ’s body and the Church, and Solomon’s prayer is a model of intercession.
lessons.question: Why is the Temple important?
lessons.activity: “Temple model” (30 min). Build a model or diagram: courts of the Gentiles, of women, of Israel, of priests; the Holy Place; the Holy of Holies. Label the altar, lamp and ark. Read 1 Kings 8:22–30. Compare it to the church building.
teach: The Temple is the place of sacrifice and God’s presence (CCC 583–586). Solomon’s dedication prayer recognizes that heaven cannot contain God (1 Kings 8:27).
Jesus honored the Temple (John 2:16) and said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” speaking of his body (John 2:19–21).
The Church is the Temple of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16; CCC 756, 797). Each baptized person is a living stone (1 Peter 2:5).
Solomon’s later idolatry led to the kingdom’s division (1 Kings 11); wisdom without fidelity is not enough.
quiz: The Temple was built by…|Solomon|Joshua|Moses|David|0|1 Kings 6.
Jesus called his body…|A boat|The Temple|A garden|A house|1|John 2:21.
The Church is also…|A club|A museum|An empire|God’s temple|3|1 Corinthians 3:16.
lessons.life: Visit a church and pray in silence.
lessons.saint: Solomon: the king who asked for wisdom and built the Temple.
lessons.mem: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16)
lessons.hook: Show a photo of a cathedral. “Why do people build beautiful places for God?” Then read 1 Kings 8:27: “Will God dwell on the earth?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how the Temple points to Christ and to the Church.

script.open: Ask, “If a genie offered you one wish, what would you ask for? What if it were God asking?”
teach: Read 1 Kings 3:5-14. Say: “God said, ‘Ask what I shall give you.’ Solomon was a young king, and he knew his limits. ‘I am but a little child; I do not know how to go out or come in.’ He asked for an understanding heart. God said, ‘Because you have asked this, and have not asked for yourself long life or riches… behold, I give you a wise and discerning mind.’ And God added what he had not asked: riches and honor. This is what Jesus taught: ‘Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things shall be yours as well.’ (Matthew 6:33)”

Read 1 Kings 6 and 8 in summary. Say: “Solomon built the Temple on Mount Moriah in Jerusalem. It was the first permanent house for God’s presence in Israel, with the ark of the covenant in the Holy of Holies. At its dedication a cloud filled the house, and Solomon prayed, ‘Will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house which I have built!’ The Temple was the center of Israel’s worship, where sacrifices were offered. It was a sign of God’s nearness.”

Say: “But Solomon did not stay faithful. He taxed heavily and allied himself with foreign nations through marriages. His wives led him to worship idols. After his death, the kingdom divided into two: Israel in the north and Judah in the south. The story warns that gifts from God can be lost when we stop following him. Wisdom is a gift, and also a habit. The Temple was destroyed later, but Jesus is the true Temple (John 2:19-21), and we are living stones of the Temple of the Spirit.”
ask: What did Solomon ask for? (An understanding heart.)
What was the Temple for? (God’s dwelling and Israel’s worship.)
What happened to Solomon in later life? (He turned to idols, and the kingdom split.)
practice: Draw a sheet with two columns: “What Solomon asked” and “What God gave.”
Fill them in from 1 Kings 3.
Draw a simple plan of the Temple: porch, Holy Place, Holy of Holies. Label the ark.
Write one sentence: “If God said, ‘Ask,’ I would ask for ___ because ___.”
script.close: Pray the prayer of Solomon: “Give your servant an understanding heart.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask God for wisdom before a decision.”

tryit: Read 1 Kings 3:5-14.
Write what Solomon asked and what God gave.
Describe what the Temple was for.
lessons.saintStory:
When David was old, his son Solomon became king. Soon afterward, at Gibeon, God appeared to him in a dream and said, “Ask what I shall give you.” Solomon answered, “Give your servant an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil.” God was pleased that he had not asked for long life, riches or victory. He gave him a wise and discerning heart, and added riches and honor besides.
Solomon’s wisdom became known. Two women came to him, each claiming to be the mother of a baby. He called for a sword to divide the child. One woman agreed; the other cried out to give the baby to the first. Solomon knew who the mother was.
He built the Temple in Jerusalem, taking seven years. But later in life, Solomon married many foreign wives and let them draw him to worship their gods. The kingdom split after he died.

lessons.title: The prophets
lessons.idea: The prophets spoke God’s word to kings and people, calling them back to the covenant, defending the poor and announcing the Messiah. Isaiah’s call and the Suffering Servant show the heart of prophecy.
lessons.question: What is a prophet’s job?
lessons.activity: “Isaiah and the Gospel” (30 min). Read Isaiah 6:1–8 (call: “Here I am, send me”) and Isaiah 53 (the Servant). Students list how Isaiah 53 matches the Passion in the Gospels (Mark 15). Write a modern “prophetic” sentence about justice.
teach: A prophet speaks for God, calling to repentance, justice and hope; not mainly predicting the future (CCC 64, 702, 2581–2584). Elijah and Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the twelve minor prophets.
Isaiah’s call (Isaiah 6) shows God’s holiness; the Sanctus at Mass echoes “Holy, holy, holy.” Isaiah 53 describes the Servant who bears our sins (CCC 601).
Jesus is the fulfillment of prophecy (Luke 24:27; CCC 711–716). John the Baptist is the last and greatest prophet (CCC 719).
Prophets suffered for the truth; the Church has prophets in every age (CCC 904–907).
quiz: Prophets speak…|For kings|God’s word|The future only|For wealth|1|CCC 64.
Isaiah 53 describes…|A suffering servant|A tax collector|A king|A warrior|0|Isaiah 53.
The prophets point to…|Egypt|Rome|The Messiah|The temple|2|CCC 711.
lessons.life: Read Isaiah 53 and a Passion narrative.
lessons.saint: Elijah: the prophet who stood against King Ahab and heard God in a whisper.
lessons.mem: “Here I am! Send me.” (Isaiah 6:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What happens when someone tells the truth to a powerful person?” Introduce the prophets as truth-tellers for God.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what a prophet does and give one example of Jesus fulfilling a prophecy.

script.open: Ask, “Is it easy or hard to tell someone a truth they don’t want to hear? Who does it for a living? In Israel, God sent prophets.”
teach: Say: “A prophet is not mainly a fortune-teller. A prophet is someone who speaks for God. The prophets reminded Israel of the covenant, called kings and people back to God, warned of the consequences of unfaithfulness, and also gave hope for the future. Often they were not welcome. Their main message was: Be faithful to God, and care for the poor. Many suffered for speaking.”

Say: “Prophets before the exile: Elijah and Elisha fought idolatry. Amos spoke against injustice: ‘Let justice roll down like waters.’ Hosea compared God’s love to a faithful husband. Isaiah saw God’s holiness and the coming Messiah (Isaiah 7:14, 9:6, 53). Jeremiah warned of the exile. After the exile, Ezekiel promised a new heart and Daniel spoke of the Son of Man. The Church reads the prophets as pointing to Jesus. John the Baptist was the last of them and the first to point out Christ.”

Say: “Elijah’s story at Horeb shows how God speaks. Elijah expected God in power, in wind, earthquake and fire. But God came in a ‘still small voice.’ God often speaks quietly, in the silence of prayer. Elijah appears again with Moses at the Transfiguration, representing the Prophets and the Law, speaking with Jesus about his Exodus in Jerusalem. The prophets prepare us to hear him.”
ask: What did the prophets do? (Spoke for God, called people back to the covenant, gave hope.)
How did God speak to Elijah? (In a still small voice.)
Who appears with Jesus at the Transfiguration? (Moses and Elijah.)
practice: Prepare cards for six prophets: Elijah, Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel. On other cards, write their messages.
Teams match each prophet to a message and a Bible reference.
Choose one and write a short summary: whom did he warn, and what did he promise?
Share with the class.
script.close: Pray in silence for one minute, listening for the still small voice. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Spend a few minutes in silence each day.”

tryit: Match each prophet to a message.
Say who they warned and what they promised.
Choose a prophet and write a one-line summary.
lessons.saintStory:
Elijah was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel, in the time of King Ahab and his wife Jezebel, who promoted the worship of the false god Baal. Elijah told Ahab there would be no rain until he said so. For three years there was a drought.
Then Elijah challenged the prophets of Baal to a contest on Mount Carmel. Each side would prepare a sacrifice, and the god who answered with fire would be God. The four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal called from morning to evening, and nothing happened. Elijah drenched his altar with water and prayed a simple prayer. Fire fell from heaven and consumed the sacrifice. The people cried, “The Lord, he is God.”
Jezebel threatened him, and Elijah fled into the desert, wishing to die. An angel fed him, and he walked forty days to Mount Horeb. There God was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in a still small voice. Elijah was later taken up in a chariot of fire.

lessons.title: The exile
lessons.idea: When Israel and Judah broke the covenant, Assyria and Babylon conquered them and many were taken into exile. God did not abandon them: the prophets promised a return and a new covenant.
lessons.question: What hope does Jeremiah give?
lessons.activity: “Letter from Babylon” (30 min). After reading Jeremiah 29:4–14, students write a letter from an exile describing their grief and hope. Include “build houses, plant gardens, seek the welfare of the city” and “I know the plans I have for you.”
teach: The northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC; Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 587 BC (2 Kings 25). The exile was a judgment and also a purification (CCC 710–711).

Jeremiah urged the exiles to settle and pray; Ezekiel promised a new heart and Spirit (Ezekiel 36:26; CCC 715). Jeremiah 31:31 promises a new covenant, which Jesus fulfills at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20).
A “remnant” returns, a theme that shapes the New Testament (CCC 711).
Link to refugees and displaced people today. Catholic social teaching calls us to welcome the stranger.
talk: Where do we feel like exiles?
quiz: Israel was taken to…|Greece|Rome|Babylon|Egypt|2|2 Kings 25.
Jeremiah told them to…|Return at once|Seek the welfare of the city|Rebel|Hide|1|Jeremiah 29:7.
The new covenant is promised in…|Psalm 23|Jeremiah 31|Job 1|Genesis 1|1|Jeremiah 31:31.
lessons.life: Pray for your city.
lessons.saint: Jeremiah: the prophet who wept over Jerusalem and promised a new covenant.
lessons.mem: “For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.” (Jeremiah 29:11)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would you take if you had to leave home in an hour?” Imagine being far from home for 70 years.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name what Jeremiah tells the exiles and what promise God makes.

script.open: Ask, “Have you ever had to move away from a home you loved, or known someone who did? What did they miss? Imagine losing your home, your church and your country.”
teach: Say: “After Solomon, the kingdom split. The northern kingdom, Israel, fell to Assyria in 722 BC. The southern kingdom, Judah, lasted longer, but kept breaking the covenant with idolatry and injustice. The prophets warned. In 587 BC, Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar captured Jerusalem, burned the Temple and took many into exile. This was the greatest crisis in Israel’s history. They had lost the land, the Temple and the Davidic king.”

Read Psalm 137:1-4.
