Say: “‘By the waters of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion.’ In exile, the people asked, ‘How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?’ Some said God had abandoned them. But the prophets said the exile was a consequence of sin, not the end. Jeremiah told them to settle and pray, because the exile would last seventy years. Ezekiel saw visions of dry bones coming to life, a promise of new life for Israel.”

Read Jeremiah 31:31-34. Say: “Jeremiah gave a promise: ‘Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel… I will put my law within them, and I will write it upon their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.’ At the Last Supper, Jesus said, ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood.’ This is the promise fulfilled. The exile taught Israel that God was with them even in a foreign land.”
ask: Why did the exile happen? (Israel broke the covenant; Babylon conquered.)
What did Jeremiah tell the exiles to do? (Settle, pray, and seek the welfare of the city.)
What did Jeremiah promise? (A new covenant written on the heart.)
practice: Draw a five-step comic: the warning, the siege, the fall of Jerusalem, the exile, the hope.
Under each, write one line.
Circle the step where God’s promise gives hope.
Read Jeremiah 29:11 and write it on a card to keep.
script.close: Pray Jeremiah 29:11 together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for people far from home.”

tryit: Tell the story of the exile in five steps.
Mark why it happened.
Read Jeremiah 29:11.
lessons.saintStory:
Jeremiah was a young man in a priestly family when God called him. “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you.” Jeremiah said, “Ah, Lord God! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth.” The Lord said, “Do not say, ‘I am only a youth.’ I am with you to deliver you.”
For over forty years he warned Judah: if they did not turn back to God and stop their injustice and idolatry, Jerusalem would fall. People did not want to hear it. He was beaten, put in stocks, thrown into a cistern, and imprisoned. He was called the weeping prophet because he grieved for his people.
In 587 BC, Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple. Many were taken to Babylon in exile. Jeremiah wrote them a letter: “Build houses and live in them… seek the welfare of the city… For I know the plans I have for you, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.”

lessons.title: Restoration
lessons.idea: After seventy years God moved Cyrus of Persia to let the Jews return. They rebuilt the Temple and the walls, and under Ezra and Nehemiah renewed the covenant by reading the Law aloud.
lessons.question: How does the community renew?
lessons.activity: “Return timeline” (25 min). Students mark key dates: 539 Cyrus, 538 first return, 516 Temple, 458 Ezra, 445 Nehemiah. Read Nehemiah 8 and act the reading of the Law (stand, listen, weep, celebrate). Compare with the Liturgy of the Word.
teach: Cyrus’ decree (Ezra 1:1–4) shows God directs history, even through pagan kings (CCC 304–306).
The returnees rebuilt the Temple and walls despite opposition. Nehemiah rallies workers, who build with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other (Nehemiah 4).
In Nehemiah 8 Ezra reads the Law; the people listen from dawn to noon, and the Levites explain. This is a model of proclaiming the Word and the homily (CCC 1154).
Many remained in the Diaspora. After this period Greek and Roman powers ruled. Judaism looked for the Messiah.
talk: How did the people respond to the Law?
quiz: Ezra read…|Psalms|A letter|The Law|Proverbs|2|Nehemiah 8.
Nehemiah rebuilt…|A ship|Babel|The wall|The ark|2|Nehemiah 2.
The people wept at…|The food|The music|The words of the Law|The trip|2|Nehemiah 8:9.
lessons.life: Read a Scripture passage aloud with your family.
lessons.saint: Nehemiah: a cupbearer who rebuilt Jerusalem’s walls in fifty-two days.
lessons.mem: “The joy of the Lord is your strength.” (Nehemiah 8:10)
lessons.hook: Show a half-built wall. Ask: “Who needs to work on it? Who needs to guard it?” Introduce Nehemiah.
lessons.assess: Ask students to retell the return and explain what Nehemiah 8 shows about God’s Word.

script.open: Ask, “What is something you took part in building with others, like a fort, a team, a garden? What went wrong? What made it work?”
teach: Say: “In 539 BC, Persia conquered Babylon. King Cyrus let the Jews return home. About fifty thousand went back and began rebuilding the Temple. It was completed in 515 BC, but it was smaller than Solomon’s, and some older people wept. The people were poor. The city had no walls. Later Ezra, a priest and scribe, returned to teach the Law, and Nehemiah, a governor, came to rebuild the city walls.”

Read Nehemiah 1-2 and 4 in summary. Say: “Nehemiah’s response was to pray first. He prayed for months. Then he acted, with courage, planning and leadership. When opposed, ‘we prayed to our God and set a guard.’ That is a good pattern: pray as if everything depends on God, and work as if it depends on you. Notice that Nehemiah did not try to do it alone. Everyone had a section.”

Read Nehemiah 8 in summary. Say: “When the wall was complete, the people gathered, and Ezra read the Law from morning till midday. The people wept as they heard it, but Nehemiah said, ‘Do not be grieved, for the joy of the Lord is your strength.’ They celebrated the feast of Booths. The return from exile was not a complete restoration. There was no king, and they were under Persian rule. The prophets looked forward to something greater, the coming of the Messiah. But Israel was a community centered on the Law and the Temple.”
ask: Who let the Jews return? (Cyrus of Persia.)
What did Nehemiah do first? (He prayed and fasted.)
What happened when Ezra read the Law? (The people wept, then rejoiced.)
practice: Pick a real project to rebuild: a clean schoolyard, a food drive, a card for a lonely neighbor.
On a sheet, list the steps and who does each (like families on each part of the wall).
List two obstacles and write a short prayer for each.
Make a one-sentence promise to start.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, strengthen the work of our hands.” (Psalm 90:17.) Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Take the first step of your project.”

tryit: Plan a rebuilding project.
List the obstacles.
Add a prayer for each.
lessons.saintStory:
Nehemiah was a Jewish man who served as cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes, far from Jerusalem. One day, his brother arrived with news: the survivors in Jerusalem were in great trouble, and the wall of the city was broken down and its gates burned. Nehemiah sat down and wept. For days he fasted and prayed.
When the king noticed his sad face, Nehemiah told him, and asked to go and rebuild. The king agreed, and sent him with letters and timber. In Jerusalem, Nehemiah inspected the walls by night, and then called the people to rebuild. Families worked on the section by their own houses. Enemies mocked them, then threatened to attack. Nehemiah set guards, and “each of the builders had his sword girded at his side while he built.”
The wall was finished in fifty-two days. Then Ezra read the Law to the people, and they renewed the covenant.

lessons.title: The Psalms and Wisdom
lessons.idea: The Psalms are Israel’s prayer book and the Church’s. They include praise, lament, thanksgiving and royal psalms. Wisdom books, like Proverbs, teach how to live: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”
lessons.question: Which psalm resonates?
lessons.activity: “Write a psalm” (30 min). Review Psalm 1 (two ways) and Proverbs 1:7. Students choose a type (praise, lament, thanks) and write their own psalm with an opening, a honest complaint or joy, and a trust statement. Share volunteers’ psalms.
teach: The Psalms are the great prayer of the Church (CCC 2585–2589). Jesus prayed them (Luke 24:44; Psalm 22 on the Cross).
Types: praise (Ps 150), lament (Ps 22, 88), thanksgiving (Ps 138), royal (Ps 2, 110), wisdom (Ps 1), pilgrim (Ps 120–134). They teach us to bring all our feelings to God.
Wisdom literature: Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Wisdom, Sirach. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7), meaning awe and reverence, not terror.
Job shows that suffering is not always punishment (CCC 309–310).
quiz: The Psalms number…|73|150|50|27|1|CCC 2585.
A lament is…|A cry of sorrow to God|A story|A feast|A law|0|Psalm 22.
Jesus quoted Psalm…|22 from the cross|23 only|1|150|0|Mark 15:34.
lessons.life: Pray a psalm each day.
lessons.saint: Ambrose: a governor who became a bishop, and who taught his people to sing the psalms.
lessons.mem: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. (Psalm 23:1)
lessons.hook: Play a short chant of a psalm or read Psalm 23 aloud. Ask, “What feelings does it express?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to give an example of lament, praise and wisdom and explain why all belong in prayer.

script.open: Ask, “If you could only use ten words to talk to God about your feelings today, what would you say? Maybe it’s anger, joy, fear, thanks. The Psalms have a prayer for each.”
teach: Say: “The book of Psalms has 150 prayers and songs, many written by David. They were Israel’s hymnbook, and Jesus prayed them. The Church prays them in the Mass and in the Liturgy of the Hours. The psalms cover every human feeling. Types include praise (Psalm 100), thanksgiving (Psalm 138), lament (Psalm 22), trust (Psalm 23), repentance (Psalm 51), and royal psalms about the king, which point to Christ (Psalm 2, 110).”

Say: “Lament psalms show that it’s allowed to bring our pain and even anger to God. Psalm 22 begins, ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ Jesus prayed it on the cross. Notice that most laments turn to trust by the end. The Psalms teach us to pray honestly. The Church also reads them as speaking of Christ: Psalm 22 describes the crucifixion, and Psalm 110 speaks of Christ’s priesthood.”

Say: “The Wisdom books are Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Wisdom and Sirach. They help us live well. Proverbs gives short sayings: ‘The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.’ Job asks why the innocent suffer; God does not explain, but shows himself. Ecclesiastes asks what is the point of life. Wisdom literature teaches that true wisdom is knowing God and living in right relationship with him, others and creation.”
ask: How many psalms are there? (150.)
Which psalm did Jesus pray on the cross? (Psalm 22.)
What does the fear of the Lord mean? (Reverent trust and awe before God.)
practice: Give each group a handful of psalms to look at: 8, 23, 51, 100, 130, 139, 22.
Sort them into types: praise, trust, repentance, lament, thanks.
Each student writes a one-line psalm of their own in one of those types.
Choose one proverb from Proverbs 10-15 to live by this week.
script.close: Pray Psalm 100 together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray one psalm each night this week.”

tryit: Sort psalms by type.
Write a lament, a praise and a thanks line.
Choose a proverb to live by.
lessons.saintStory:
Ambrose was born around 340 into a Roman family, and became governor of northern Italy, based in Milan. When the bishop of Milan died, there was a dispute about who should be chosen. Ambrose went to the church to calm the crowd. A child cried out, “Ambrose for bishop!” and the crowd took it up. He was not even baptized. He tried to refuse, but was baptized, ordained and consecrated bishop within a week.
He studied Scripture and the Fathers with energy. He preached so powerfully that Augustine came to hear him. When Arians threatened to take a church in Milan, he and his people barricaded themselves inside, singing hymns and psalms to pass the time. He wrote hymns that are still sung.
Ambrose confronted the emperor Theodosius over a massacre, and required him to do public penance. He died in 397. He loved the psalms: “In the psalms we meet the whole of human life.”

units.title: Preparing for the Messiah
units.eq: How did the Old Testament point to Christ?

lessons.title: The promises of the Messiah
lessons.idea: The prophets promised a Messiah: born in Bethlehem, of a virgin, a king from David’s line, a suffering servant. The New Testament shows Jesus fulfilling these promises.
lessons.question: Which prophecies are fulfilled?
lessons.activity: “Prophecy and fulfillment chart” (30 min). Students match: Isaiah 7:14 / Matthew 1:22–23; Micah 5:2 / Matthew 2:5–6; Isaiah 9:1–2 / Matthew 4:14–16; Isaiah 53:5 / 1 Peter 2:24; Psalm 22:16–18 / John 19:23–24, 37; Zechariah 9:9 / Matthew 21:4–5. Discuss: Why does it matter that these were written long before?
teach: The prophets prepare for the Messiah (CCC 522–524, 711–716). Messiah (Hebrew) and Christ (Greek) mean “anointed.”
Different strands: a king (Psalm 2, Isaiah 9), a servant (Isaiah 53), a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), a priest (Psalm 110), a Son of Man (Daniel 7). Jesus unites them (CCC 436, 439–440).
Not every prophecy is a prediction. Matthew shows that history and Scripture find their meaning in Christ (CCC 128–130).
Be honest that some connections are deeper than literal. The Church reads the Old Testament in light of Christ.
quiz: Micah foretold the Messiah’s birth in…|Bethlehem|Cana|Jerusalem|Nazareth|0|Micah 5:1.
Isaiah 7:14 speaks of…|A tree|A queen|The virgin who will conceive|A flood|2|Matthew 1:23.
Fulfilment means…|A rule|Prophecy abandoned|A coincidence|Prophecy realized in Christ|3|CCC 128.
lessons.life: Create a chart of three prophecies.
lessons.saint: John the Baptist: the last prophet, who pointed to the Lamb of God.
misc: “The prophets wrote with Jesus’ name in mind.”
“Jews were wrong not to see it.”
lessons.mem: “But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah… from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel.” (Micah 5:2)
lessons.hook: Show a pair of puzzle pieces. “Prophecy and fulfillment fit.” Read Micah 5:2 and Matthew 2:1–6.
lessons.assess: Ask students to give three prophecies with their fulfillments.

script.open: Ask, “If you were told that a great leader was coming, how would you prepare? What would you want to know in advance? Israel waited centuries for a Messiah.”
teach: Say: “Messiah means ‘anointed one’; in Greek, Christ. Kings, priests and prophets were anointed with oil. Israel looked for one anointed by God to save them. The prophets gave promises about him. He would be born of the line of David (2 Samuel 7:12-16, Isaiah 11:1). He would be born in Bethlehem (Micah 5:2). A virgin would conceive and bear a son, Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14). He would be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6).”

Say: “Other promises were stranger. Isaiah 53 describes a servant who is ‘despised and rejected,’ ‘wounded for our transgressions,’ who ‘bore the sin of many.’ Psalm 22 describes a righteous sufferer whose hands and feet are pierced and whose garments are divided. Zechariah 9:9 describes a king riding a donkey. Daniel 7 has a ‘son of man’ receiving an everlasting kingdom. Together, they portray a Messiah who is both glorious king and suffering servant. It took Jesus’ life to show how those fit.”

Say: “After the exile came about four hundred years with no prophets. Then John the Baptist appeared. Jesus said that he was Elijah who was to come. He prepared the way. The Gospels often say events happened ‘to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet.’ After the Resurrection, Jesus walked with two disciples on the road to Emmaus and ‘beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.’ (Luke 24:27) That is how the Church reads the Old Testament: as pointing to Christ.”
ask: What does Messiah mean? (Anointed one.)
Name two prophecies about the Messiah. (Born in Bethlehem; a virgin will conceive; suffering servant.)
What did Jesus do on the road to Emmaus? (Explained the Scriptures that spoke about himself.)
practice: Make a two-column chart: Prophecy and Fulfillment.
Fill in rows: Micah 5:2 / Matthew 2:1; Isaiah 7:14 / Matthew 1:22-23; Zechariah 9:9 / Matthew 21:1-5; Psalm 22:18 / John 19:23-24; Isaiah 53:5 / 1 Peter 2:24.
Add one that you find yourself.
Choose the one that surprises you most, and say why.
script.close: Pray the Benedictus (Luke 1:68-79) or: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read one prophecy and its fulfillment with your family.”

tryit: Collect messianic prophecies.
Match each to its fulfillment in Jesus.
Explain what was promised.
lessons.saintStory:
John the Baptist was the son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth, born when they were old, after an angel announced his birth. Zechariah was struck mute for doubting, and when the baby was born and named John, his tongue was loosed, and he prophesied.
John lived in the desert, wearing camel hair and eating locusts and wild honey. Crowds came to him at the Jordan, where he called them to repent and be baptized. He said, “I baptize you with water; but he who is mightier than I is coming.” When Jesus came, John said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”
He baptized Jesus, then told his own disciples to follow him. “He must increase, but I must decrease.” John told King Herod that it was wrong to take his brother’s wife, and was imprisoned and beheaded.

lessons.title: Types of Christ
lessons.idea: A type is a person, event or thing in the Old Testament that foreshadows Christ. Adam, Isaac, Moses, the manna, the bronze serpent and Jonah all point to him. The New Testament is hidden in the Old; the Old is made clear in the New.
lessons.question: What is a type?
lessons.activity: “Match types” (25 min). Cards: Adam (Romans 5:14), Isaac (Genesis 22), Moses (Deuteronomy 18), manna (John 6:31–35), bronze serpent (John 3:14–15), Jonah (Matthew 12:40), Melchizedek (Hebrews 7), the Temple. Students match each with Jesus and say what they share.
teach: Typology: the Old Testament’s persons and events are real and also point forward (CCC 128–130). “The New is hidden in the Old and the Old is unveiled in the New” (St Augustine).
Hebrews 8–9 explains that the earthly priests and tabernacle were a shadow of the heavenly (Hebrews 8:5). Christ is the high priest and the sacrifice (CCC 1544).
Adam is “a type of the one who was to come” (Romans 5:14). Jesus is the new Adam; Mary is the new Eve (CCC 411).
Warn gently against reading everything as a type; use the Church’s tradition as a guide.
quiz: Manna foreshadows…|Confession|Baptism|Marriage|The Eucharist|3|John 6:31-35.
The bronze serpent foreshadows…|The Cross|A king|The ark|A flood|0|John 3:14.
Adam is a type of…|Moses|David|Satan|Christ|3|Romans 5:14.
lessons.life: Look for a type of Christ in tonight’s reading.
lessons.saint: Justin Martyr: a philosopher who found in the Old Testament the Christ he had been searching for.
misc: “Typology makes the Old Testament less real.”
lessons.mem: “These are a shadow of what is to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.” (Colossians 2:17)
lessons.hook: Show a shadow of an object and ask what it is. Then reveal the object. “The Old Testament cast shadows; Jesus is the reality.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain one type and its fulfillment.

script.open: Show a map with a road sign pointing to a city. Ask, “Is the sign the same as the city? What is the sign for?” Say, “The Old Testament is full of signs pointing to Christ.”
teach: Say: “Typology is the Church’s way of reading the Old Testament. A type is a person, event or thing in the Old Testament that points ahead to something greater in Christ, called the antitype. The type has its own meaning in its own time, and it is also a preview. The Church Fathers, such as Justin, loved typology. St. Augustine said, ‘The New Testament lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is made clear in the New.’”

Say: “Here are some types. Adam is a type of Christ, the new Adam (Romans 5). Abel, the innocent man killed, is a type of Christ. Noah’s ark prefigures the Church, and the flood prefigures Baptism. Isaac carrying wood for his own sacrifice prefigures Jesus carrying the cross (Genesis 22). Joseph, betrayed by his brothers and raised up, is a type of Christ. Moses, the lawgiver and liberator, prefigures Christ; the Passover lamb prefigures the Lamb of God; the manna prefigures the Eucharist (John 6); the bronze serpent lifted up prefigures the cross (John 3:14); David prefigures the Messianic king; Jonah, three days in the fish, prefigures the burial and Resurrection (Matthew 12:40).”

Say: “Melchizedek, the priest-king who brought out bread and wine for Abraham (Genesis 14), prefigures Christ the priest and the Eucharist. In every case, the fulfillment is greater than the type. Jesus is the true Lamb, true bread, true temple. Typology doesn’t make the Old Testament less real. It shows that God’s plan has one author and one center: Christ.”
ask: What is a type? (A person or event in the Old Testament that points to Christ.)
What does the manna point to? (The Eucharist.)
What does the bronze serpent point to? (The cross.)
practice: Prepare cards with types: Adam, Isaac, Joseph, Passover lamb, manna, bronze serpent, Jonah, Melchizedek. On other cards, put their fulfillments.
Teams match the cards.
Write one sentence for each pair: “Like ___, Jesus ___, but greater because ___.”
Draw one pair on a sheet.
script.close: Pray: “Lord Jesus, you are the fulfillment of all the Scriptures.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Find a type of Christ in the Old Testament reading at Mass.”

tryit: Match each type to Christ.
Say how the type is like and unlike him.
Draw one pair.
lessons.saintStory:
Justin was born around the year 100 in Samaria, to pagan parents. He studied one philosophy after another, looking for the truth: Stoic, Pythagorean, Platonic. One day, walking by the sea, he met an old man who talked to him about the prophets, who were older than the philosophers and had foretold Christ. Justin said that a fire was kindled in his soul.
He became a Christian but kept wearing the philosopher’s cloak, and opened a school in Rome. He wrote to the emperor to defend Christians against false charges. In his First Apology he gave the earliest detailed description of the Mass outside the New Testament: the readings, the homily, the prayers, the bread and wine, and the collection for the poor.
He also argued that the Old Testament pointed to Christ. In about 165, he was arrested with some of his students, and beheaded for refusing to sacrifice to the gods.

lessons.title: The Old Testament in the liturgy
lessons.idea: At Mass the Old Testament is proclaimed and prayed: the first reading is chosen to harmonize with the Gospel, and the responsorial psalm answers it. Jesus read Isaiah in the synagogue and declared, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
lessons.question: Which readings do you remember?
lessons.activity: “This Sunday’s first reading” (25 min). Look up this Sunday’s readings. Students identify the first reading, psalm and Gospel, find the link, and write one sentence on how they connect. Then pray the psalm aloud together.
teach: The Old Testament is part of the Church’s liturgy (CCC 1093–1095). The Church reads it as the preparation for Christ and sees the Eucharist as the fulfillment (CCC 1094).
The Sunday cycle (A, B, C) and the Easter Vigil’s seven readings give a sweep of salvation history (CCC 1154). The first reading usually fits the Gospel theme.
The responsorial psalm is a meditation on the first reading. The Church’s hymns also use the psalms and canticles.
The Old Testament is not obsolete (CCC 121–123). Marcionism, which rejected it, was condemned.
talk: Why does the Church read the Old Testament?
quiz: The first reading is usually from…|Revelation|The Old Testament|A letter|The Gospel|1|CCC 1093.
The responsorial psalm responds to…|The first reading|The creed|The Gospel|The homily|0|GIRM.
The Church reads the Old Testament because…|It is short|It is easy|It is old|It prepares for Christ|3|CCC 121.
lessons.life: Compare this Sunday’s first reading and Gospel.
lessons.saint: Ephrem the Deacon: a poet who taught the Church to sing its faith.
misc: “We skip the Old Testament because it’s harsh.”
lessons.mem: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” (Luke 4:21)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 4:16–21 and ask what Jesus did with the scroll. “He is the key to the Scriptures.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to identify the three readings in a given Sunday and explain how they connect.

script.open: Ask, “If you went to Mass and the first reading, from the Old Testament, was about a lamb, and the Gospel was about Jesus feeding the crowd, would you think there’s a link? Let’s see why the Church chooses readings together.”
teach: Say: “At Sunday Mass there are usually three readings plus a psalm. The first reading is usually from the Old Testament (during Easter, from Acts). The responsorial psalm responds to the first reading. The second reading is from the letters or Revelation. The Gospel is the high point. The first reading is chosen to fit the Gospel. The Old Testament prepares for Christ and the Gospel reveals him. This follows what Jesus himself did on the road to Emmaus.”

Say: “The readings follow a three-year cycle for Sundays: Year A (Matthew), Year B (Mark, with John in the summer), and Year C (Luke). Weekdays have a two-year cycle for the first reading. Over the cycle, the Church reads most of the Bible. The Church year also shapes the readings: Advent looks to the coming of the Savior, and the prophets (especially Isaiah) are read; Lent recalls the story of salvation, and the Easter Vigil reads from Genesis, Exodus and the prophets.”

Say: “The Old Testament is also found throughout the prayers. The responsorial psalm, the Holy, Holy, Holy (Isaiah 6), the Lamb of God (Exodus 12 and John 1:29), the Our Father, and the mention of Abel, Abraham and Melchizedek in the Eucharistic Prayer all come from it. The Easter proclamation, the Exsultet, sings of Passover and of Adam’s ‘happy fault.’ When we understand the Old Testament, we pray the Mass better.”
ask: Why is the first reading chosen? (It fits the Gospel.)
How many years is the Sunday cycle? (Three: A, B and C.)
Name an Old Testament prayer we use at Mass. (Holy Holy Holy, Psalms, Lamb of God.)
practice: Give each pair the readings for a recent or upcoming Sunday.
Read the first reading and the Gospel.
Write a sentence that shows how the first reading prepares for the Gospel.
Share, and then look for the type (like manna and the bread of life).
script.close: Pray the psalm from the Sunday readings together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read the first reading and the Gospel before Mass.”

tryit: Map a Sunday’s readings.
Show how the Old Testament reading fits the Gospel.
Write the connection in one sentence.
lessons.saintStory:
Ephrem was born around 306 in Nisibis, in what is now Turkey, and lived in Syria. He became a deacon, never a priest, and taught in schools and wrote hymns in Syriac. In his time, false teachers were spreading their views in songs. Ephrem wrote orthodox hymns to the same tunes, and had choirs of women and men sing them.
His hymns are full of images from Scripture. He wrote about the Virgin Mary, the cross, Paradise and the Eucharist. He called Christ the “medicine of life,” and likened the Church to Noah’s ark and a harp that the Spirit plays.
When the city of Edessa was struck by famine, he organized aid for the poor. He died in 373. He is called the “Harp of the Spirit” and a Doctor of the Church. Ephrem shows how Scripture and worship are woven together.

units.title: Living the Old Testament faith today

lessons.title: The Ten Commandments for today
lessons.idea: The Ten Commandments still guide life today: in friendships, school, technology, family and money. They are a path of love, summed up by Jesus in two commands. Applying them takes thought and conscience.
lessons.question: How do they apply now?
lessons.activity: “Debate the scenario” (30 min). Teams get cases (online rumors, cheating, ignoring a lonely classmate, Sunday sports, gossip) and decide which commandments apply, what a loving response is, and what it costs. Present to class.
teach: The Commandments are a path of love with a positive core (CCC 2052–2074). Each prohibition protects a good and implies a duty.

Applications: first commandment, putting God first (also over gadgets); second, respecting God’s name; third, Sunday; fourth, family; fifth, respect for life including bullying; sixth and ninth, purity; seventh, honesty and fairness; eighth, truth online; tenth, contentment (CCC 2083–2557).
Grave sins can be committed in the heart as well as in deed (Matthew 5:21–30). Conscience must be formed (CCC 1783).
Ask students to apply them with courage, not fear.
talk: How does a commandment apply to social media?
quiz: Natural law is…|Church law only|A law of physics|The moral law known by reason|Civil law|2|CCC 1954.
The Commandments are…|Optional|Cultural|Temporary|Always binding|3|CCC 2072.
The Decalogue summarizes…|Temple rites|Love of God and neighbor|Taxes|Rules of war|1|CCC 2055.
lessons.life: Apply one commandment to your online behavior.
lessons.saint: Maximilian Kolbe: a friar who took the place of a condemned man.
misc: “If no one gets hurt it’s not a sin.”
lessons.mem: “If you love me, you will keep my commandments.” (John 14:15)
lessons.hook: Describe a school scenario: a friend asks you to share answers during a test, or posts a rude picture online. “Which commandment is in play?”
lessons.assess: Present a new scenario and ask students to apply two commandments and propose a loving response.

script.open: Ask, “Which is harder: to not do something wrong, or to do something good? Which is the commandment’s aim?”
teach: Say: “The commandments can sound like a list of ‘don’ts.’ But each protects something precious, and Jesus shows what they ask of us positively. The Catechism teaches that each commandment says ‘no’ to something in order to say ‘yes’ to love. The first three: no other gods means put God first and worship him. Do not take his name in vain means treat God’s name with reverence. Keep the Sabbath means set time for God each week. Honor your father and mother means respect and gratitude toward family and legitimate authority.”

Say: “The fifth commandment, do not kill, protects the dignity of every human life from conception to natural death, and also asks us to avoid hatred and to build peace. The sixth, do not commit adultery, protects marriage, faithfulness and purity. The seventh, do not steal, protects property and asks us to share and be honest in work. The eighth, do not bear false witness, protects the truth and others’ good name. The ninth and tenth, do not covet, guard the heart from envy and greed, since sin begins within.”

Say: “Jesus said that the Law could be summed up in two commandments, love of God and love of neighbor. A teenager asked, ‘What good deed must I do to have eternal life?’ Jesus said, ‘If you would enter life, keep the commandments.’ (Matthew 19:17) The commandments are not outdated; they are the basic guide to how to love. Each one of us should know them, and use them in our examination of conscience before Confession.”
ask: What do the commandments protect? (God’s honor, life, family, truth, property and the heart.)
What did Jesus say sums up the Law? (Love of God and love of neighbor.)
How do we use the commandments? (In our examination of conscience.)
practice: Divide the class into ten groups. Each takes one commandment.
They write on a poster: what it forbids, what it asks of us positively, and a modern example (including online life).
Present to the class.
Each student chooses one to practice this week.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, teach me your ways.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Use the commandments to examine your conscience tonight.”

tryit: Rewrite each of the commandments as a positive.
Add a modern example.
Choose one to practice.
lessons.saintStory:
Raymond Kolbe was born in Poland in 1894. As a boy he had a vision in which Mary offered him two crowns, white for purity and red for martyrdom, and he said he would take both. He joined the Franciscans, taking the name Maximilian, and started a movement and a magazine to honor Mary. He went to Japan as a missionary and founded a friary in Nagasaki.
In World War II, he was arrested by the Nazis for hiding Jews and Poles in his friary. He was sent to Auschwitz. In July 1941, a prisoner escaped, and the camp commander chose ten men to be starved to death in revenge. One of them, Franciszek Gajowniczek, cried out for his wife and children.
Father Kolbe stepped forward and said, “I am a Catholic priest. I wish to take his place.” He led the men in prayer in the starvation bunker for two weeks, and was finally killed with an injection on August 14, 1941. Gajowniczek survived and lived into his nineties. Kolbe was named a saint in 1982.

lessons.title: Justice and mercy
lessons.idea: The prophets demanded justice for the poor and mercy for the weak. “Let justice roll down like waters.” Catholic social teaching continues this call: human dignity, the common good, solidarity and care for the poor.
lessons.question: What does God require?
lessons.activity: “Justice project” (30 min). Students identify a need (hunger, loneliness, creation) and plan a project with Micah 6:8 as its motto: do justice, love kindness, walk humbly. Fill in who, what, when, and how prayer will support it.
teach: Amos, Isaiah and Micah condemned empty worship without justice (Amos 5:21–24; Isaiah 1:11–17). God hears the cry of the poor (CCC 2443–2446).
Catholic social teaching has principles: dignity of the person, the common good, subsidiarity, solidarity, preferential option for the poor (CCC 1905–1912, 2443–2449).
Justice gives each their due; mercy goes beyond it. Together they reflect God (CCC 1807, 2447).
Link to the works of mercy and to Pope Francis’ call to care for the poor.
quiz: Micah 6:8 says to do justice, love mercy and…|Walk humbly|Sing|Rest|Fight|0|Micah 6:8.
Amos wanted justice to…|Be taxed|Be hidden|Be silent|Roll down like waters|3|Amos 5:24.
The poor are…|Close to God’s heart|Lazy|Ignored|Dangerous|0|CCC 2448.
lessons.life: Do a justice project this month.
lessons.saint: Dorothy Day: a journalist who founded the Catholic Worker and fed the hungry.
lessons.mem: “He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8)
lessons.hook: Show a photo of a food line or a homeless shelter. Read Amos 5:24 and ask, “What is God asking?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Micah 6:8 and name one way to live it.

script.open: Ask, “What is the difference between giving someone a fish, teaching them to fish, and asking why they can’t get to the river? Can you do all three?”
teach: Say: “The prophets cared about justice. Amos said, ‘Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.’ (Amos 5:24) They spoke against cheating the poor, bribing judges, mistreating widows, orphans and foreigners. Micah 6:8 says, ‘What does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?’ These come together.”

Say: “Justice means giving each person what is due, especially basic rights: food, shelter, work and dignity. Mercy goes beyond that: it meets need with compassion. We need both. Charity gives food to the hungry; justice asks why people are hungry. The Church teaches the preferential option for the poor: care for those in need comes first. Catholic social teaching has principles such as the dignity of the human person, the common good, solidarity, and care for creation.”

Say: “Jesus in the synagogue of Nazareth read from Isaiah: ‘He has anointed me to bring good news to the poor… to proclaim release to the captives… to set at liberty those who are oppressed.’ (Luke 4:18) This is his mission. The Church continues it. And Jesus said that we will be judged by how we treated the least of his brothers and sisters. The Old Testament’s call for justice has not ended. The Law of Moses even had provisions for the poor: leaving some of the harvest for them to glean (Leviticus 19:9-10), and the Jubilee year.”
ask: What does the prophet Micah say God requires? (Do justice, love kindness, walk humbly with God.)
What is the difference between justice and mercy? (Justice gives what is due; mercy goes beyond with compassion.)
What is one principle of Catholic social teaching? (Dignity of the person, common good, solidarity, option for the poor.)
practice: Give small groups a short situation: a classmate has no lunch; a neighbor is evicted; a factory pays unfair wages.
For each, name what mercy would do now and what justice would ask about the cause.
Choose one real need in your school or town and plan one action.
Share your plan.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, make me an instrument of your peace and justice.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do one act of mercy this week.”

tryit: Match a prophet’s message to a modern situation.
Distinguish justice from mercy.
Plan one action.
lessons.saintStory:
Dorothy Day was born in 1897 in Brooklyn, New York. She became a journalist and a radical, writing for causes of the poor and workers. She was jailed for demonstrating for women’s right to vote. Though she was not religious, she was drawn to the Catholic Church by the faith of poor immigrants, and she was baptized in 1927 after the birth of her daughter.
She asked God to show her how to use her gifts for the poor. In 1933, with Peter Maurin, she started a newspaper, the Catholic Worker, which sold for a penny, and opened houses of hospitality in New York where people could find food and shelter. Soon there were houses across the country. She lived among the poor.
She was a pacifist and was arrested many times for protests. She prayed daily, went to Mass often and made retreats. She died in 1980. Her cause for canonization has been opened. She said, “I really only love God as much as I love the person I love the least.”

lessons.title: Prayer with the psalms
lessons.idea: Lectio divina is a way to pray with Scripture: read, meditate, pray, contemplate. Praying the Psalms with Jesus and with the Church unites our voices to the prayer of millions.
lessons.question: Which psalm do you use?
lessons.activity: “Lectio with a psalm” (25 min). Lead Lectio divina with Psalm 23: read slowly, notice a word; read again and meditate on it; pray in response; rest in silence; resolve a small action. Journal a line from the experience.
teach: Lectio divina has four moments: lectio (read), meditatio (reflect), oratio (pray), contemplatio (rest), and often actio (act) (CCC 2705–2708).
The Psalms give words to every human emotion and are Christ’s own prayer, which we pray in him (CCC 2587–2589). Psalm 51 teaches repentance; Psalm 23 trust.
The Church prays the Psalms in Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours (CCC 1174–1178).
Encourage a daily habit: one psalm a day, or the Sunday psalm all week.
quiz: Lectio divina begins with…|Speaking|Singing|Sleeping|Reading|3|CCC 2708.
Psalm 23 begins…|Blessed is the man|The Lord is my shepherd|Out of the depths|Have mercy|1|Psalm 23.
Psalm 51 is…|A harvest song|A wedding song|A battle song|A penitential psalm|3|Psalm 51.
lessons.life: Pray Psalm 23 or 51 nightly.
lessons.saint: Bernard of Clairvaux: a monk who prayed the psalms every day and wrote about the love of God.
misc: “I need to feel something to pray.”
lessons.mem: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How can the same words mean something new each time you read them?” Show Psalm 23 and invite silence.
lessons.assess: Ask students to walk through the four steps of Lectio divina and share a word or phrase from the psalm.

script.open: Ask, “What do you do when you don’t know what to say in prayer? The Church has a prayer-book that gives us the words: the Psalms.”
teach: Say: “Because Jesus prayed the psalms, and the Church has prayed them for two thousand years, praying them joins us to Christ’s own voice. The Catechism says the psalms are the masterwork of prayer in the Old Testament (CCC 2585). We can pray them aloud or silently, alone or together. The Church also teaches that when we pray a psalm, Christ prays in us and with us.”

Say: “Here is a way to pray a psalm slowly, in four steps. First, read the psalm slowly, aloud or silently. Second, meditate: stop at a word or line that stands out. Repeat it. What does it mean? Third, pray: answer God. Thank him, ask, say sorry, or simply stay with him. Fourth, rest: be still for a minute, and let God act. This follows the monastic tradition called lectio divina, sacred reading, which Bernard and the monks practiced.”

Say: “You can match a psalm to your mood. Afraid: Psalm 23 or 91. Sorry: Psalm 51 or 130. Thankful: Psalm 100 or 136. Angry or sad: Psalm 13 or 42. Amazed by creation: Psalm 8 or 104. In the evening: Psalm 4 or 141. Many psalms end with praise even when they begin with pain. Learning even a few by heart, and praying them regularly, gives us words for every season of life.”
ask: Why do we pray the psalms? (Jesus prayed them; the Church prays them; they cover every feeling.)
What are the four steps? (Read, meditate, pray, rest.)
Which psalm could you pray when you are afraid? (Psalm 23 or 91.)
practice: Give each student Psalm 23 or 130 on a sheet.
Guide them through the four steps: read slowly, underline a line, write a prayer, then sit in silence for one minute.
Share one line that stood out.
Choose a psalm to pray each day this week.
script.close: Pray Psalm 23 together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray a psalm before you sleep.”

tryit: Pray a psalm in the four steps.
Write what each step gave you.
Choose a psalm for the week.
lessons.saintStory:
Bernard was born around 1090 to a noble family in Burgundy, France. When he was twenty-two, he persuaded thirty relatives and friends to join him at the poor monastery of Cîteaux. Within three years he was sent to found a new monastery at Clairvaux, which grew to hundreds of monks. He lived very strictly and became ill.
He prayed the psalms every day in the monastic Hours, and he wrote eighty-six sermons on the Song of Songs, describing the soul’s love for God. He loved the psalms for their depth and for the way they join our experience to God’s word. He wrote, “The measure of love is to love without measure.”
Bernard advised popes and kings, but remained a monk. He died in 1153. He shows what praying the psalms can do: join us to Christ’s own prayer.

units.title: The first three commandments
units.eq: How do we love God above all?

lessons.title: You shall have no other gods
lessons.idea: The first commandment calls us to love God above everything and to put nothing in his place. We worship God alone and avoid idols, superstition and fear of luck.
lessons.question: What does it mean to put God first?
lessons.activity: List things people put first (sports, popularity, money, devices). Draw a ladder with God at the top and talk about how to keep the order.
teach: The first commandment: “I am the Lord your God… you shall have no other gods before me” (CCC 2083–2094). It calls for faith, hope and love of God above all.
We adore God alone and worship him (CCC 2096–2100). Sins against it: idolatry, superstition, divination, magic, tempting God, irreligion and atheism (CCC 2110–2128).
Idols today can be money, fame, pleasure or technology (CCC 2113). Even good things become idols when they come first.
Images of Christ and the saints are not idols; we honor the person, not the object (CCC 2131–2132).
talk: What things try to take first place in your life?
What is the difference between honoring a saint and worshiping God?
Why is horoscope-reading a problem for a Christian?
quiz: The first commandment asks us to…|Love God above all|Tell the truth|Honor parents|Take a rest|0|CCC 2083.
An idol is…|Anything we put before God|A prayer|A statue only|A saint|0|CCC 2113.
Praying to a saint is…|Wrong|Asking for help, not worship|Worship|Magic|1|CCC 956.
lessons.life: Choose one thing that takes too much of your time and give some of that time to prayer or service.
lessons.saint: Thomas More: a lawyer and chancellor who put God before the king.
lessons.mem: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.” (Deuteronomy 6:5)
lessons.hook: Ask students to rank four things from most to least important in their lives. Ask what happens when the order changes.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the first commandment and give a modern example of an idol.

script.open: Ask, “If a stranger looked at your calendar, phone and room, what would they say you love most?” Let students think quietly. “That is a good test of what we worship.”
teach: Read Exodus 20:1-6. Say: “‘I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no other gods before me.’ The first commandment says that God alone is to be adored. We owe him faith, hope, love and worship. Jesus said, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.’ (Matthew 4:10)”

Say: “Ancient peoples carved statues. Today our idols may be money, popularity, sports, screens, success, power or pleasure. An idol is anything we put in the place of God, anything we trust to save us. Good things become idols when we make them ultimate. Sins against the first commandment include superstition, such as trusting horoscopes, charms or fortune-telling; the occult and attempts to contact spirits; sacrilege, which is disrespect for holy things; and atheism or indifference, ignoring God. Faith is the response to this commandment.”

Say: “What does the first commandment ask? To believe in God, hope in him, love him with all our heart, and worship him in prayer and in the Mass. It’s not just a ban. It’s an invitation to the best thing in life. Augustine prayed, ‘You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you.’ Thomas More shows that sometimes to keep this commandment takes courage.”
ask: What does the first commandment ask? (To worship God alone and love him above all.)
What is an idol? (Anything we put in the place of God.)
Name a sin against the first commandment. (Superstition, the occult, sacrilege, atheism, indifference.)
practice: Make a class list of modern idols.
Sort them under: “promises happiness,” “promises safety,” “promises approval.”
Write beside each: What does God offer instead?
Rewrite the first commandment as a prayer in your own words.
script.close: Pray the Act of Faith or: “My Lord and my God.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Put God first today in one choice.”

tryit: List modern idols.
Sort them by what they promise.
Write the first commandment as a prayer.
lessons.saintStory:
Thomas More was born in London in 1478. He became a lawyer, a scholar and a friend of Erasmus, and wrote a book called Utopia. He married, had four children, and filled his house with learning. He rose to be Lord Chancellor of England, the king’s highest official, in 1529.
King Henry VIII wanted to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, and when the pope refused, he broke with Rome and declared himself head of the Church in England. Thomas resigned as chancellor. He refused to sign an oath accepting the king as head of the Church, and was imprisoned in the Tower of London for over a year. His daughter Margaret visited him.
At his trial, he was condemned. On the scaffold, in 1535, he said that he died “the king’s good servant, but God’s first.” He was named a saint in 1935.

lessons.title: You shall not take the name of the Lord in vain
lessons.idea: The second commandment asks us to respect God’s name and the names of holy people and things. We use God’s name to pray, bless and praise, not to curse or swear falsely.
lessons.question: How can we honor God’s name?
lessons.activity: Write a list of ways to use God’s name well (prayer, blessing, thanks) and ways to avoid misuse. Practice the Sign of the Cross with reverence and say the name of Jesus slowly.
teach: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (CCC 2142–2149). God’s name is holy, and we show respect in speech and silence.
Sins against it: blasphemy, cursing, careless use of God’s name, false oaths (perjury) (CCC 2148–2155). Oaths and promises made in God’s name must be kept (CCC 2150–2155).

The name of Jesus is powerful in prayer: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10; CCC 2666–2668). We bless God’s name in the Sign of the Cross and our personal name given in Baptism is holy (CCC 2156–2159).
Treat this topic with understanding: many children have heard careless language at home. Teach what to say instead.
talk: Why do you think people use God’s name carelessly?
How does the Sign of the Cross honor God’s name?
quiz: The second commandment forbids…|Misusing God’s name|Lying|Missing Sunday|Stealing|0|CCC 2142.
A false oath is called…|Perjury|Praise|Fasting|Prayer|0|CCC 2152.
We honor God’s name when we…|Shout|Hide|Curse|Pray and bless|3|CCC 2143.
lessons.life: Catch yourself using God’s name carelessly and replace it with a short prayer.
lessons.saint: Bernardine of Siena: a preacher who taught people to honor the name of Jesus.
lessons.mem: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow.” (Philippians 2:10)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How would you feel if a stranger shouted your name as an insult?” Introduce the second commandment.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the second commandment and two ways to honor God’s name.

script.open: Say a student’s name with respect, then with contempt. Ask, “What changed? A name stands for the person. What about God’s name?”
teach: Read Exodus 20:7. Say: “‘You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.’ God’s name is holy. In the Bible, a name is not just a label but a person’s identity. When God revealed his name to Moses, it was a gift of closeness, and the Jews are so reverent that they will not say it. The second commandment calls us to honor God’s name, and the names of Jesus, Mary and the saints.”

Say: “What breaks this commandment? Blasphemy, which is speaking against God, Jesus, Mary or the saints with contempt. Cursing, which is calling down evil in God’s name. Using God’s name casually, such as ‘Oh my God’ as an exclamation. False oaths: swearing to something false, or breaking a promise made in God’s name. Jesus said, ‘Let what you say be simply Yes or No.’ (Matthew 5:37) Oaths are allowed when needed, such as in court, but must be truthful. Also, using God’s name to justify violence or hatred.”

Say: “What honors the name? Praying it with reverence. Making the Sign of the Cross, which begins in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Bowing our head at the name of Jesus. Praising: ‘Blessed be the name of the Lord.’ The Jesus Prayer: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.’ Paul writes, ‘At the name of Jesus every knee should bow.’ (Philippians 2:10) The name Jesus means ‘God saves.’ Our own baptismal name is also holy: we are baptized in the name of the Trinity and carry the name Christian.”
ask: What does the second commandment ask? (To honor and respect God’s name.)
What are some ways it is broken? (Blasphemy, cursing, careless use, false oaths.)
What does the name Jesus mean? (God saves.)
practice: Write ways of using God’s name on cards: “Praying the Our Father,” “Saying OMG as a joke,” “Making a promise before God,” “Cursing,” “Bowing at the name of Jesus,” “Lying under oath,” “Praising.”
Sort into two piles: honors the name or dishonors it.
Talk about how to replace careless words.
Write a short prayer to the holy name, such as the Jesus Prayer.
script.close: Pray the Jesus Prayer five times slowly. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Notice how you use God’s name this week and bow at the name of Jesus at Mass.”

tryit: Sort ways of using God’s name.
Say which honor it and which dishonor it.
Write a prayer of the Holy Name.
lessons.saintStory:
Bernardine was born in 1380 in Tuscany, Italy. He was orphaned young and cared for by his aunt. As a young man, when the plague struck Siena, he helped nurse the sick at the hospital for months and almost died. He then joined the Franciscans in 1402.
Bernardine became a famous preacher. Huge crowds came to hear him, so many that he had to preach in open squares. He spoke in everyday language, with humor and stories, against gambling, vanity, feuds and cursing. He urged people to settle disputes and make peace.
He promoted devotion to the holy name of Jesus. He would hold up a tablet with the letters IHS, the first letters of Jesus’ name in Greek, surrounded by rays of light, and people would kneel. He died in 1444.

lessons.title: Remember the Sabbath: keep the Lord’s Day holy
lessons.idea: The third commandment asks us to set aside a day for God. Christians keep Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, with Mass, rest, family and works of mercy.
lessons.question: Why do Christians keep Sunday?
lessons.activity: Plan a Lord’s Day that includes Mass, rest, a family activity and one work of mercy. Compare with how your family spends Sundays now.
teach: The Sabbath recalls creation and the Exodus (CCC 2168–2172). Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man” (Mark 2:27), and he healed on it.
Christians keep Sunday because Jesus rose on the first day of the week (CCC 2174–2176). Sunday Mass is required for Catholics unless a serious reason prevents it (CCC 2180–2183).
We rest from unnecessary work to worship, enjoy family, and perform works of mercy (CCC 2184–2188). Rest respects human dignity.
Be sensitive: some families must work on Sundays or lack transportation. Talk about desire for Mass and what they can do.
talk: What makes a day feel set apart?
What activities fill up Sunday that could be left out?
What is one work of mercy you could do on Sunday?
quiz: Christians keep Sunday because…|A king decided|Moses said so|It is the weekend|Jesus rose on that day|3|CCC 2174.
The Church requires Catholics to…|Pray all day|Never work|Attend Mass on Sundays and holy days|Fast every Sunday|2|CCC 2180.
“The Sabbath was made for man” means…|It does not matter|Work is bad|Rest is a punishment|Rest is a gift|3|Mark 2:27.
lessons.life: Choose one thing to leave undone on Sunday so there is room for rest, family and Mass.
lessons.saint: Isidore the Farmer: a laborer who began every day at Mass.
lessons.mem: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.” (Exodus 20:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “When was the last time you had a whole day to rest with no rush?” Let them describe it.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain why Sunday matters and plan one practice for it.

script.open: Ask, “When was the last time you had a whole day with no school, no chores, and nothing you had to do? What would that day be for?”
teach: Read Exodus 20:8-11 and Genesis 2:2-3. Say: “‘Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labor… but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God.’ God rested after creation, blessed the seventh day and made it holy. The Sabbath is a gift, a day for worship, family and rest. The Israelites were slaves in Egypt who never had a day off. God made them free, and gave them a day of rest.”

Say: “For Christians, the Lord’s Day is Sunday, the day of the Resurrection. It is the first day of the week and also the ‘eighth day’ of new creation. The Church obliges Catholics to attend Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation, and to avoid unnecessary work. This is a serious obligation; missing Mass without a good reason (like illness) is a grave sin. Mass is where we meet the risen Lord, hear his word and receive his Body. The early Christians said, ‘We cannot live without Sunday.’”

Say: “Sunday is also for rest, family and joy: time with family and friends, meals, play, visits to the sick, acts of charity, time in nature, quiet reading and prayer. Jesus said, ‘The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.’ (Mark 2:27) Rest is not wasted time; it is a sign that we are not slaves to work and productivity. Today it is easy to fill Sunday with activities and screens. A holy Sunday takes planning. Isidore went to Mass first, then worked, and trusted God to provide.”
ask: Why do Christians keep Sunday? (The day of the Resurrection.)
What does the Church require on Sundays? (Mass and rest from unnecessary work.)
Is rest wasted time? (No, it is a gift and a sign of trust in God.)
practice: Draw a plan for a Lord’s Day: morning, Mass, meal, afternoon, evening.
Include worship (Mass, prayer), rest (play, quiet), family (a meal, a game), and service (visit or call someone).
Mark one thing you will give up on Sunday to make it special, such as chores, extra screen time or shopping.
Share your plan with a partner.
script.close: Pray: “This is the day the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.” (Psalm 118:24.) Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Make a family Sunday plan.”

tryit: Plan a Lord’s Day.
Include Mass, rest, family and service.
Mark what you will give up.
lessons.saintStory:
Isidore was born around 1070 in Madrid, Spain, to poor parents. He worked as a farm laborer on the estate of a wealthy landowner, Juan de Vargas, and spent his life in the same fields. He married a woman named Maria, who is also honored as a saint, and they had a son who died young.
Isidore went to Mass before work each morning, and prayed as he plowed. Some of the other workers complained to the landowner that Isidore was arriving late. When Juan went to look, he saw an angel plowing alongside Isidore, according to the old story.
Isidore was generous with the little he had, sharing his food with the poor and even feeding the birds in winter. He died in 1130 and was named a saint in 1622. He is the patron of farmers. His life shows how to put God first in a day of work.
